articles.title: Surging Tanker Rates Buoy Bahri Profit
articles.summary: Saudi Arabian shipping company Bahri reported a sharp increase in third-quarter and nine-month earnings for 2026, benefiting from higher very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight rates, increased chartering activity and shifting trade patterns…
articles.body: Surging Tanker Rates Buoy Bahri Profit Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 28, 2026 Copyright Timon/AdobeStock Saudi Arabian shipping company Bahri reported a sharp increase in third-quarter and nine-month earnings for 2026, benefiting from higher very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight rates, increased chartering activity and shifting trade patterns amid continued disruption in the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea. Net profit for the first nine months reached SAR 9.98 billion ($2.66 billion), up 587% year-on-year, on revenue of SAR 26.10 billion ($6.96 billion), an increase of 268%. Third-quarter net profit climbed 891% to SAR 5.09 billion ($1.36 billion), while revenue increased 504% to SAR 14.83 billion ($3.95 billion). Bahri Oil was the principal earnings driver, benefiting from stronger realized VLCC rates and additional chartered tonnage deployed to meet customer demand. The company's chemicals, integrated logistics and dry bulk businesses also reported revenue growth. The financial gains came despite security incidents affecting four Bahri-owned vessels during the first nine months, resulting in the deaths of two crew members. Two vessels have returned to service following repairs, while two remain under repair. Bahri continued expanding its fleet, acquiring three secondhand medium gas carriers to enter the LPG and ammonia transportation market. The first was delivered in September, with the remaining vessels expected by early 2027. Its owned fleet stood at 107 vessels at September 30. Following the quarter, Bahri signed a SAR 1.692 billion ($451 million) agreement with International Maritime Industries to build three VLCCs for delivery between 2029 and 2030. "Looking ahead, we are entering the next phase of Bahri's growth from a position of strength," said CEO Ahmed Ali Al Subaey. Operating cash flow rose 83% to SAR 4.07 billion ($1.09 billion), while net debt declined to SAR 8.16 billion ($2.18 billion). Its net debt-to-EBITDA ratio improved to 0.59 from 2.11 a year earlier.

articles.title: The Business of Offshore CO₂ Storage: A New Market for Maritime Infrastructure
articles.summary: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is moving from a collection of demonstration projects toward a new infrastructure business. As of July 2025, 734 commercial CCS facilities were in operation or development, up from 628 a year earlier, while…
articles.body: The Business of Offshore CO₂ Storage: A New Market for Maritime Infrastructure Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Alisa Reiner , Contributor Alisa Reiner is an independent contributor. Alisa brings experience in both... October 28, 2026 Copyright VectorMine/AdobeStock Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is moving from a collection of demonstration projects toward a new infrastructure business. As of July 2025, 734 commercial CCS facilities were in operation or development, up from 628 a year earlier, while total capture capacity in the pipeline increased from 416 million tons per annum (Mtpa) to 513 Mtpa (64 Mtpa operational) (Figure 1). Figure 1. Cumulative operating CCS facilities by region, 1972-2025 Source: Intelatus Global Partners’ interpretation of Global CCS Institute data. The number of operating facilities rose from 50 to 77 between 2024 and 2025, while 657 facilities were in different development stages in 2025 (Figure 2). Figure 2. CCS facilities project pipeline, year-on-year change, 2024-2025 Source: Intelatus Global Partners’ interpretation of Global CCS Institute data. Commercially, this matters because more projects are moving from studies toward physical assets, contracted services, and long-duration operations. Growth Is Shifting Toward Offshore-Capable Regions An independent Intelatus Global Partners review identifies eight operating facilities and seven facilities under construction involving offshore CO₂ injection for geological storage or enhanced oil recovery (EOR), as of 2025. Europe is emerging as a leading market for shared networks and offshore storage development – its dedicated CO₂ transport-and-storage projects doubled between 2023 and 2024. To the East, in Asia, CNOOC commissioned China’s first offshore CCUS project at the Enping 15-1 oilfield in 2025. The project is expected to inject more than 1 Mt of CO₂ over the following decade for EOR while increasing crude-oil production by around 200,000 tons. To the West, in the Americas, Petrobras’ Santos Basin pre-salt project provides an established offshore precedent, reinjecting 14.2 Mt of CO₂ into the basin’s pre-salt reservoirs in 2024, capturing EOR-associated CO₂. Together, these developments show a strong fit between CCS growth and the existing offshore energy ecosystem. But for maritime and offshore companies, the opportunity lies less in capture equipment than in what happens after capture. Depending on the transport mode, CO₂ must be dehydrated and compressed for dense-phase pipeline transport, or liquefied, refrigerated, and stored for marine transport. It then requires receiving, injection, monitoring, and long-term stewardship arrangements. As storage shifts offshore, ships, ports, pipelines, wells, platforms, and subsea systems connect industrial emitters with the reservoir, creating a new offshore value chain and potentially a new commodity flow. Offshore Storage Models Are Diversifying Storage geology shapes the business model. Depleted oil and gas reservoirs benefit from existing subsurface data on pressure, porosity, and permeability and may allow wells or pipelines to be reused. Saline formations offer larger potential resources but usually require more appraisal and new infrastructure. The former can lower development uncertainty and capital needs; the latter can support larger dedicated storage hubs. Table 1. Selected offshore CO₂ storage developments Project Region Annual capacity Offshore model Northern Lights Norway 1.5 Mtpa (to at least 5 Mtpa) Ship-to-terminal, subsea pipeline to offshore saline reservoir Porthos Netherlands 2.5 Mtpa Pipeline, reused offshore platform/wells and depleted gas fields Greensand Future Denmark 0.4 Mtpa (potentially 4-8 Mtpa) Dedicated CO₂ carrier to offshore platform and depleted oil field Northern Endurance Partnership United Kingdom 4.0 Mtpa (potentially 10-23 Mtpa) Offshore pipelines to saline aquifer; all-subsea injection system Liverpool Bay CCS United Kingdom 4.5 Mtpa (potentially 10 Mtpa) Repurposed offshore gas infrastructure and depleted fields Kasawari CCS Malaysia 3.7 Mtpa Integrated offshore gas-field CCS with storage in a depleted reservoir Sources: Northern Lights; Porthos; Greensand Future / INEOS; bp / Northern Endurance Partnership; Eni; PETRONAS; IEA. Northern Lights achieved first injection in August 2025, receiving liquefied CO₂ at Øygarden by ship and sending it through a 100-kilometer pipeline into the Aurora reservoir around 2,600 meters below the seabed in the Norwegian North Sea. The project demonstrates a commercial model in which ships deliver CO2 from multiple industrial customers to a common coastal terminal and offshore storage system. Greensand Future takes a different route – CO₂ is aggregated at the Port of Esbjerg and shipped to the Nini field in the Danish North Sea. The vessel acts as a virtual pipeline for emitters outside a fixed network. Pipelines concentrate spending upfront in fixed assets, while shipping carries more operating costs through liquefaction, fuel, storage, and cargo handling. That makes ships more flexible as volumes and destinations are evolving, while pipelines are better suited to large, predictable flows. Eni’s Liverpool Bay system repurposes parts of existing offshore infrastructure and depleted gas reservoirs around 30 kilometers offshore. For mature basins, CCS can therefore extend the economic role of reservoirs, wells, and pipelines after hydrocarbon production declines. In the Northern Endurance Partnership project, CO₂ from Teesside and the Humber industrial cluster will move through two offshore pipelines to the Endurance saline aquifer, where all installed infrastructure will be subsea, including manifolds, flowlines, and six injection wells. Porthos has advanced construction of its onshore and offshore transport system and well-conversion program, but in April 2026 pushed start-up to no earlier than the second half of 2027. This demonstrates that while reuse reduces greenfield requirements, it does not remove integration risk. Kasawari in Malaysia provides yet another model – CCS integrated directly with offshore gas production. PETRONAS plans to capture CO₂ from the high-CO₂ Kasawari gas field offshore Sarawak and reinject around 76 Mt over the project life. A New Offshore Commodity The legal framework is also becoming more workable. The London Protocol, the 1996 IMO treaty governing disposal of wastes and other materials at sea, adopted a 2009 amendment permitting cross-border export of CO₂ for sub-seabed storage; in 2019, parties approved provisional application before formal entry into force. That matters because the best storage sites may lie in a different country from the emissions source. Transporting CO₂ also requires a different physical chain from conventional bulk shipping. Pipeline systems typically compress CO₂ into a dense phase, while marine transport requires liquefaction and refrigerated storage before loading. That means the maritime opportunity extends beyond the vessel itself to compression and liquefaction systems, storage tanks, pumps, loading equipment, and terminal infrastructure. Ports can therefore become carbon hubs. CO₂ from multiple capture sites can be consolidated at coastal terminals for conditioning, temporary storage, and onward transport. Ports serving refinery, chemical, cement, and power clusters are natural aggregation points. When Sharing Becomes Good Business This supports a hub-and-cluster model in which several emitters share transport and storage infrastructure. For lower-volume sources such as individual cement plants, a dedicated pipeline and storage system may be uneconomic – aggregation can therefore expand the addressable CCS market, not merely reduce unit costs. Maritime industry players should pay attention to the development of terminals aggregating volumes, CO₂ carriers connecting dispersed sources, and storage systems serving multiple customers. Transport and storage can become a standalone infrastructure business based on contracted capacity and long-term service agreements. Northern Lights already follows this model, offering third-party emitters across Europe access to an integrated transport-and-storage network. Policy Is Creating Storage Demand The European Union (EU) Net-Zero Industry Act requires developing at least 50 Mtpa of annual CO₂ injection capacity in the EU by 2030. In May 2025, the European Commission identified 44 obligated entities expected to contribute to that target. This shifts the CCS discussion from whether storage capacity should be developed to how quickly it can be permitted, financed, and connected to emitters. That raises the strategic value of offshore expertise. Oil and gas companies bring reservoir models, seismic data, well inventories, and operating systems while contractors contribute drilling, subsea engineering, compression, flow assurance, and integrity capabilities. Ports and shipowners connect dispersed capture sites with concentrated offshore storage. The Main Risk Is the Chain Porthos illustrates a key CCS risk – all parts of the system must come online together. Delays in pipelines, compression, wells, capture facilities, or permitting can leave completed assets underused and postpone revenues across the whole project. This type of integration risk is familiar across many maritime and offshore projects. However, unlike oil or LNG, captured CO₂ usually has little or no intrinsic sale value at destination in dedicated-storage chains. Revenues instead come from transport-and-storage fees, carbon-price incentives, regulated support, or the compliance value created for the emitter. CO₂ used for EOR or other applications can generate additional revenue, but this is not the core business model for most dedicated storage hubs. Storage is also a long-duration service, with obligations extending from site characterization through monitoring, post-injection surveillance, and eventual closure. Because operators recover costs through transport and storage services rather than the sale of a commodity, asset utilization and contracted throughput are critical to project economics. Anchor customers, long-term contracts and shared infrastructure therefore become central to project finance. The Next Offshore Market Carbon sequestration is creating a new infrastructure market rather than simply adding another piece of equipment to industrial plants. The value chain reaches from ports and specialized ships to subsea pipelines, repurposed platforms, injection wells, reservoir management, and decades of monitoring. Not all CCS spending will move offshore, but the direction is clear – as the market scales, a growing share of the commercial opportunity extends beyond capture into transport and dependable, permitted storage. For maritime and offshore companies, CO₂ is becoming a new cargo, a new subsurface service and a new use for aging infrastructure.
takeaways: The Business of Offshore CO₂ Storage: A New Market for Maritime Infrastructure Maritime Activity Reports, Inc.

articles.title: India Approves $1.05B Plan to Boost Shipping Container Production
articles.summary: India has approved a $1.05 billion (100 billion rupee) scheme aimed at increasing domestic shipping container manufacturing capacity around tenfold to 750,000 TEUs annually, as the country seeks to reduce import dependence and strengthen its…
articles.body: India Approves $1.05B Plan to Boost Shipping Container Production Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 28, 2026 © tiero / Adobe Stock India has approved a $1.05 billion (100 billion rupee) scheme aimed at increasing domestic shipping container manufacturing capacity around tenfold to 750,000 TEUs annually, as the country seeks to reduce import dependence and strengthen its maritime supply chains. The Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme (CMPS), approved by the Union Cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on October 28, will support the establishment of new manufacturing facilities and expansion of existing production units. The initiative, first announced in the 2026–27 Union Budget, is intended to establish an internationally competitive container manufacturing industry and position India as a potential global export hub. The largest component of the scheme provides approximately $935 million (88.91 billion rupees) in operational expenditure assistance for containers manufactured to global shipping standards and sold by eligible manufacturers. Approximately $90 million (8.59 billion rupees) of additional funding is earmarked for interest subvention assistance, providing a 3% annual interest subsidy on eligible term loans for new manufacturing facilities and expansion of existing capacity. The scheme also allocates approximately $16 million (1.5 billion rupees) to support shared testing and certification facilities, including dynamic longitudinal impact testing. The government estimates that the program could generate 3,000 direct jobs and more than 50,000 indirect jobs, while supporting related industries such as specialized steel, corner castings, wooden frames and paints.

articles.title: Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system
articles.summary: A Norwegian-led consortium involving shipbuilder Vard and offshore vessel owner Island Offshore is preparing to build and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system, targeting its first vessel deployment in 2031 or 2032. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, will...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Norway lines up full-scale test of marine nuclear propulsion system Bojan Lepic October 28, 2026 0 0 1 minute read A Norwegian-led consortium involving shipbuilder Vard and offshore vessel owner Island Offshore is preparing to build and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system, targeting its first vessel deployment in 2031 or 2032. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, will move from engineering studies to physical integration and testing, with a full-scale test facility planned at Stette near Ålesund in 2027. The project will combine Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MW electric Gem microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems. The initial testing phase will use electric heating instead of nuclear fuel to simulate reactor operation, allowing engineers to assess how the propulsion system performs under realistic vessel operating conditions. Tests will examine normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, system stress, emergency responses and interaction with ship crews. The consortium includes Vard Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk. Vard will handle ship design and integration, while Vard Electro will develop power management and automation systems. Island Offshore will contribute operational expertise and plans to become the first shipowner to install the technology on an offshore vessel. The initiative builds on the NTNU-led NuProShip research programme, which has been examining the feasibility of integrating advanced nuclear reactors into commercial shipping. Earlier this year, Vard presented a nuclear-powered offshore construction vessel concept developed through NuProShip II, examining reactor integration, operational requirements and safety considerations. The latest pilot has received NOK20m ($2m) from the Research Council of Norway, while its initial development stage is expected to cost approximately NOK150m ($15.6m), including partner contributions. Although the project is targeting commercial demonstration early in the next decade, actual vessel deployment will depend on completing technical qualification and obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Map displaying Atlantic margin-focused Sintana's portfolio of assets Source: Sintana Energy Canada-headquartered oil and natural gas exploration player Sintana Energy has put a deal in place to bring a full cash-out of $900,000 forward to conclude its exit from all remaining Trinidad assets before the year is out. Sintana Energy has confirmed that the first installment of $450,000 in deferred consideration for the sale of its business in Trinidad in 2025 has been received. The exact identity of the buyer that purchased the firm's Trinidad assets remains undisclosed. The company agreed with the unnamed purchaser a variation of terms for the deferred consideration payment installments, such that full payment of all outstanding amounts, less an agreed early payment discount, would be accelerated to the end of December 2026. Sintana will now get aggregate cash payments totalling $900,000 in respect of the deferred balance for the sale, while the remaining deferred consideration payments, which previously extended through to the end of 2027, were originally expected to amount to $1 million. As a result, the company anticipates fully concluding the exit from all business, assets, and operations in Trinidad by year-end. The firm remains focused on frontier and offshore exploration and development. Sintana’s asset portfolio is located in offshore basins in Namibia , Uruguay , and Angola, alongside historical or legacy assets in places like Colombia and the Bahamas, following the closing of its chapter in Trinidad. articles.title: Europe’s container ports: Why is transshipment falling while gateway traffic grows?
articles.summary: Europe’s major container ports are reporting increasingly contrasting traffic patterns in 2026, with headline throughput figures concealing significant changes in the composition of cargo flows. At Rotterdam and Valencia, transshipment volumes have declined substantially during the first nine months of the year,...
articles.body: Europe’s major container ports are reporting increasingly contrasting traffic patterns in 2026, with headline throughput figures concealing significant changes in the composition of cargo flows. At Rotterdam and Valencia, transshipment volumes have declined substantially during the first nine months of the year, while traffic linked to imports and inland markets has strengthened. Antwerp-Bruges presents a different picture, with modest overall container growth driven by empty rather than full containers. The figures raise an important question for Europe’s port sector: are changes in terminal capacity, cargo demand and shipping networks altering the balance between transshipment and gateway activity? The available evidence points to changes at individual ports rather than a confirmed Europe-wide shift. Rotterdam: Terminal capacity reshapes cargo flows According to the Port of Rotterdam Authority’s nine-month results , container throughput increased by just 0.1% in TEUs during January–September 2026, while containerised cargo measured in tonnes declined by 2.2%. Behind the relatively stable headline figure, however, two sharply different trends emerged. Transshipment throughput fell by 20%, while hinterland container volumes increased by 7.2%. Full-container imports serving inland markets rose by 8.9%, compared with growth of just 1% in full-container exports. The explanation provided by the port authority is particularly significant. Long-standing capacity constraints at Rotterdam’s deep-sea terminals have resulted in more cargo being handled through alternative ports, freeing capacity for containers moving to and from the hinterland. This suggests that Rotterdam’s changing cargo mix cannot be attributed solely to shifts in underlying demand. Terminal capacity and operational constraints are also influencing which cargo flows remain within the port. As Container News reported , the decline in transshipment has occurred alongside continued growth in inland-linked traffic. For terminal operators and shipping lines, the distinction matters. Transshipment containers depend heavily on vessel connections and network design, whereas gateway cargo also relies on inland distribution infrastructure and access to regional markets. Rotterdam’s results therefore illustrate how operational limitations can influence the balance between these activities without producing a comparable decline in total TEUs. Valencia: Stronger imports, weaker transshipment Valencia is experiencing a similar divergence in traffic categories, although the available figures do not establish the same underlying cause. According to Valenciaport’s September traffic report , total container throughput declined by 0.91% during the first nine months of 2026, reaching approximately 4.2 million TEUs. Full-container imports increased by 10.02% to 856,431 TEUs, while full-container exports rose marginally by 0.31% to 681,113 TEUs. In contrast, full containers handled in transshipment fell by 9.81% to 1,552,065 units. The difference is substantial. Valencia is recording stronger inbound container activity while losing volume in a segment that remains central to its position within Mediterranean shipping networks. However, the latest monthly figures introduce an important qualification. During September alone, full-container transshipment declined by just 0.82%, a considerably smaller reduction than the cumulative nine-month figure. Meanwhile, full-container imports increased by 11.68% and exports by 5.68%. As highlighted in Container News’ coverage of Valenciaport’s latest results , September’s performance suggests that the earlier decline in transshipment was moderating. This makes it premature to describe Valencia’s weaker transshipment performance as a permanent structural change. Unlike Rotterdam, where the port authority explicitly identified terminal capacity constraints, Valencia’s published figures do not establish a single comparable explanation for the reduction. Antwerp-Bruges: More TEUs do not necessarily mean more full containers The Port of Antwerp-Bruges’ nine-month results provide a third perspective on Europe’s changing container traffic. Total container throughput increased by 1.2% in TEUs, supported by a strong recovery during the third quarter. Yet full-container throughput declined by 1.3%, while empty-container movements increased by 11.7%. The port authority linked this development to rising import volumes and pressure on exports, which increased the need to reposition empty equipment, particularly towards Asia. This distinction demonstrates why total TEU growth cannot automatically be interpreted as an equivalent increase in laden cargo activity. A port can report higher container volumes while handling fewer full containers, depending on the balance between imports, exports and empty-equipment movements. Antwerp-Bruges also illustrates a limitation of direct port comparisons. Its published nine-month figures do not provide the same transshipment breakdown available for Rotterdam and Valencia. Consequently, its performance is useful for understanding the changing composition of European container traffic, but not for establishing whether transshipment is declining across the region. What the differences mean for European port competition Taken together, the three ports reveal a more complex picture than their aggregate throughput growth rates suggest. Rotterdam’s transshipment decline is explicitly associated with deep-sea terminal capacity constraints. Valencia combines weaker cumulative transshipment with stronger imports and a recent moderation in the decline. Antwerp-Bruges shows how empty-container repositioning can support overall TEU growth even as full-container traffic contracts. These developments also highlight the importance of distinguishing actual container movements from the nominal vessel capacity deployed by shipping lines. Changes in service rotations and port calls may influence future traffic distribution, but announced network capacity cannot be treated as evidence of equivalent cargo volumes. For European ports, the competitive implications will depend on whether current changes persist, how terminal capacity develops and whether shipping lines continue adjusting their networks. The next reporting periods will be particularly important for Valencia, where September’s figures suggest improving transshipment performance, and for Rotterdam, where capacity constraints remain a documented factor. The central finding is not that Europe’s ports are collectively moving away from transshipment. It is that the relationship between transshipment, gateway cargo and total container throughput is becoming increasingly important to understanding their individual performance.
takeaways: Europe’s major container ports are reporting increasingly contrasting traffic patterns in 2026, with headline throughput figures concealing significant changes in the composition of cargo flows.
At Rotterdam and Valencia, transshipment volumes have declined substantially during the first nine months of the year, while traffic linked to imports and inland markets has strengthened.
Antwerp-Bruges presents a different picture, with modest overall container growth driven by empty rather than full containers.

articles.title: Damaged Tanker Leaks Oil Across UAE Waters as Spill Widens
articles.summary: An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation…
articles.body: Damaged Tanker Leaks Oil Across UAE Waters as Spill Widens Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 28, 2026 Illustration © Yellow Boat / Adobe Stock An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns. Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated October 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank. The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished. The images provided by the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker. Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution. "The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Center, told Reuters. In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice. The UAE's marine life "is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website. (Reuters - Reporting by Vinaya K and Federico Maccioni, Editing by William Maclean)

articles.summary: Russia expects to begin regular year-round eastbound shipping along the Northern Sea Route in early 2027, as additional nuclear icebreaker capacity, newer ice-class LNG carriers and pressure to redirect energy exports toward Asia bring the long-delayed ambition closer to reality.

(Source: Atomflot) Russia expects to begin regular year-round eastbound shipping along the Northern Sea Route in early 2027, as additional nuclear icebreaker capacity, newer ice-class LNG carriers and pressure to redirect energy exports toward Asia bring the long-delayed ambition closer to reality. Vladimir Panov, head of the Arctic Directorate at state nuclear corporation Rosatom, said that preparations for regular winter voyages were in their final stages. The planned start will coincide with one of Russia’s largest shippers beginning regular eastbound deliveries, he said, without identifying the company. Panov pointed to Novatek’s substantial LNG shipments along the route, as well as the start of oil exports from Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project . Six voyages carrying Vostok Oil cargoes have already been completed, he said. “[The Northern Sea Route] is one step away from regular shipments in the eastern direction, that is, one step away from year-round navigation,” Panov said, adding that Rosatom expects the transition to take place in early 2027. The timing would be significant for Novatek, Russia’s largest LNG producer. From Jan. 1, 2027, the European Union’s ban on Russian LNG imports under long-term contracts is scheduled to take effect , increasing the incentive to direct cargoes toward Asian buyers. Regular eastbound shipments would allow the company to move more LNG from its Arctic production facilities toward Asia without relying exclusively on seasonal navigation windows. Russia is also expanding its icebreaker fleet. The nuclear-powered Chukotka , the fourth serial Project 22220 icebreaker, is scheduled to enter service in early 2027, bringing the total number of operational nuclear icebreakers to nine , according to Panov. The additional capacity would complement a growing fleet of Arc7 ice-class LNG carriers, including newer-generation vessels designed for demanding winter conditions. Russia’s Zvezda shipyard has delivered two 2nd generation Arc7 gas carriers optimized for winter navigation. Winter navigation along the NSR is not new. In January 2021, Novatek sent several Arc7 LNG carriers through the eastern route, including Christophe de Margerie and Nikolay Yevgenov . While the former completed its passage without reported issues, Nikolay Yevgenov suffered damage to one of its three azimuth propulsion units near the Bering Strait, illustrating the mechanical risks associated with winter ice navigation. Further trials demonstrated that winter exports were technically possible. In December 2022 and January 2023, the Arc7 carrier Vladimir Voronin completed a round trip between the Yamal LNG terminal at Sabetta and China in 42 days, with nuclear icebreaker support during parts of the voyage. Arc7 carriers have also made late-spring voyages in May and early June. However, the most difficult late-winter period, particularly March and April, has remained a significant operational challenge. Russia previously aimed to establish year-round eastbound navigation in early 2024, with Rosatom and Novatek announcing the plan in 2023 . The proposed regular service did not materialize as scheduled, despite the successful trial voyages and changes to navigation rules that expanded the periods during which Arc7 vessels could sail independently. The conditions are now more favorable in several respects. Additional Project 22220 icebreakers are entering service, newer Arc7 vessels offer improved winter capabilities, and the loss of access to the EU market for Russian LNG under long-term contracts creates a stronger commercial incentive to develop winter routes. Yet the technical and logistical constraints remain. Panov acknowledged that increasing convoy speeds is a priority and that Russia must continue expanding emergency-response, communications and medical infrastructure along the route. articles.title: Containership orderbook heads towards 16m teu
articles.summary: The containership industry’s extraordinary ordering spree is showing no signs of slowing, with the global orderbook now exceeding 15m teu and another wave of megamax contracts poised to push the total towards 16m teu before the end of the year. The latest figures from Alphaliner show that approximately 40 additional...
articles.body: Containers Operations Containership orderbook heads towards 16m teu Sam Chambers October 28, 2026 0 420 2 minutes read The containership industry’s extraordinary ordering spree is showing no signs of slowing, with the global orderbook now exceeding 15m teu and another wave of megamax contracts poised to push the total towards 16m teu before the end of the year. The latest figures from Alphaliner show that approximately 40 additional large containerships are expected to join the newbuilding pipeline, involving Maersk, Yang Ming, CMA CGM and MSC. Orders from the first two carriers are expected shortly, while contracts involving CMA CGM and MSC are believed to have been signed but have yet to be confirmed by Alphaliner. Among the most significant prospective deals is Maersk’s return to the largest containership segment. Alphaliner reports that the Danish carrier is negotiating exclusively with Chinese shipyards for a series of twelve LNG dual-fuel vessels of 24,000 teu, potentially accompanied by options for another twelve. At an estimated $240m apiece, the initial programme would be worth approximately $2.88bn, rising to $5.76bn if all options were exercised. The ships would represent Maersk’s first entry into the 24,000 teu category, moving beyond the distinctive twin-engine Triple-E designs it introduced more than a decade ago. Chinese yards are being favoured on cost and available construction slots. The orderbook’s expansion is particularly striking against the size of the existing fleet. Alphaliner’s October Monthly Monitor put contracted capacity at 15.12m teu, equivalent to 43.9% of the trading fleet. Its projections show fleet capacity expanding by 9.2% in 2027 and a further 14.4% in 2028. That supply wave is arriving just as the industry’s operating geography undergoes another fundamental change. Sea-Intelligence reported this week that around 60% of deployed Asia-Europe capacity is now operating, or scheduled to operate, via Suez rather than around the Cape of Good Hope. Assuming security conditions permit, the consultancy expects further normalisation during the first quarter of 2027. Returning to shorter voyages will release effective vessel capacity into a market already facing accelerating physical deliveries. Braemar warned in its latest container briefing that the combination of returning Suez services and the expanding orderbook was “not an ideal combination for charter rates”. Jefferies has expressed similar caution over 2027, warning that newbuilding deliveries could push fleet growth ahead of cargo demand. Yet today’s charter market remains remarkably resilient. Alphaliner reports that only 0.8% of the global cellular fleet was commercially idle in its latest survey, while charter rates have climbed to their highest levels in four years. Promptly available ships remain exceptionally scarce, with some large units reportedly commanding six-figure daily earnings. The ordering boom is also reshaping propulsion choices. LNG dual-fuel ships now represent 56% of contracted capacity, compared with 12% for methanol dual-fuel vessels. Conventional propulsion accounts for just under 32%. Alphaliner recorded 2.3m teu of fresh LNG dual-fuel orders during 2026, with the anticipated megamax contracts potentially adding another 1m teu. Methanol ordering, by contrast, has almost stalled. For now, geopolitical disruption and tight prompt vessel availability continue to underpin exceptional charter earnings. But Alphaliner cautioned that the coming delivery avalanche “will eventually take its toll on the market”. articles.summary: Shipping may be enjoying one of its strongest booms in decades, but the extraordinary profits generated by geopolitical turmoil are raising difficult questions about risk, investment and what happens when the wars end, delegates at yesterday’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco heard. Opening the event at the Yacht Club de...
articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Maritime CEO Forum: Shipping’s wartime boom tests discipline Splash October 28, 2026 0 258 2 minutes read Splash Splash Shipping may be enjoying one of its strongest booms in decades, but the extraordinary profits generated by geopolitical turmoil are raising difficult questions about risk, investment and what happens when the wars end, delegates at yesterday’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco heard. Opening the event at the Yacht Club de Monaco, Splash editor Sam Chambers asked whether today’s riches were encouraging owners to repeat the mistakes of past cycles. Burak Cetinok, head of research at Arrow, described the rally as unusually broad across freight, vessel values and sale-and-purchase activity. VLCC earnings this month were 14 times their 10-year average, he calculated, with the weekly multiple approaching 20. The latest peak was four times that of 2007-08. Despite the eye-watering numbers, Cetinok saw no immediate sell signal in conventional shipping. His biggest concern was fresh capacity: Arrow’s analysis suggested that once an orderbook reaches roughly 25% of the existing fleet, earnings have historically tended to fall within 24 to 36 months. Svein Moxnes Harfjeld, chief executive of DHT Holdings, was more sanguine about the VLCC orderbook. By the end of 2029, he said, almost half the fleet would be over 15 years old and a quarter over 20, creating considerable replacement demand. With tanker owners generally carrying much less debt than before the 2008 crash, he argued, the industry was also more resilient. For DHT, avoiding boom-time exuberance meant sticking to internal “traffic lights” governing investment and risk, even when high spot rates made restraint look costly. Illustrating the desperation to secure oil supplies, Harfjeld described a refinery customer accepting a voyage 40 days longer, at a 50% higher freight rate, to avoid heightened Red Sea risks. Gus Majed, founder and group chief executive of Paratus, said the surge in tanker earnings was a rational response to the breakdown of established energy routes and refining markets. But the frequency of attacks was making returns less attractive after adjusting for risk. “Returns are starting to compress on a risk-adjusted basis,” he said, warning that governments and companies were reassessing energy security and strategic stockpiles. A flattening between spot and forward freight rates would be one sign that the boom was losing momentum. René Kofod-Olsen, chief executive of V.Group, warned that record earnings should not obscure operational vulnerabilities. Some owners were still managing fleets of “10, 20, 30 ships on WhatsApp and the occasional e-mail”, he said, while cyberattacks on vessels and offices underscored the need for investment in systems and training. Above all, he urged owners not to treat seafarers and technical management as commodities. From the floor, Andy Dacy of JP Morgan Asset Management cautioned against chasing ships at the top of the market and suggested public and private owners might react differently when valuations turned. Another delegate, Lars-Christian Svensen, who heads Bruton, Himalaya Shipping and OMC Tankers, countered that flexibility mattered more than identifying as a spot or long-term player. Owners needed to be nimble and prepared to sell into strength. Tomorrow, Splash will bring readers details from yesterday’s tanker session at the exclusive shipowner gathering on the Cote d’Azur. articles.body: Americas Europe Regulatory Tankers Sanctioned Russian tankers head for US carrying diesel Sam Chambers October 28, 2026 0 270 1 minute read PTP LLC PTP LLC Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are heading towards the United States under the controversial agreement between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, with Moscow preparing to dispatch a fourth vessel today. Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak confirmed yesterday that three shipments were underway, despite mounting opposition from US lawmakers who argue the deal breaches existing legislation prohibiting Russian energy imports. According to vessel tracking data from Kpler, the ships are Talisman, Leruo and Agioi Fanendes, carrying a combined 924,000 barrels of diesel. Two of the tankers are subject to international sanctions. The Talisman is sanctioned by the US and European Union, while Leruo appears on British and EU sanctions lists. The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes, managed by Greek interests, loaded approximately 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. The three ships departed Primorsk between October 16 and 22 and are expected to reach the US Atlantic coast between November 7 and 11, although their declared destinations remain subject to change. Novak said the shipments demonstrate that Moscow and Washington are implementing their agreement despite political opposition. The Trump administration issued a six-month sanctions exemption earlier this month, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel until April 7 next year. The concession is intended to help alleviate soaring US fuel prices, which have been driven higher by the Iran conflict and disruptions to global refining and shipping. However, the agreement has created a legal and political confrontation. A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has warned banks, ports and energy companies against handling the cargoes, arguing that the Treasury exemption cannot override legislation passed in 2022 banning imports of Russian petroleum products. European and British sanctions on Russian petroleum imports also remain in force, complicating the movements of sanctioned vessels through international waters. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Greater China Shipyards Meadway Bulkers splashes out on ultramax series in China Adis Ajdin October 28, 2026 0 208 1 minute read Meadway Bulkers Meadway Bulkers Greek dry bulk owner Meadway Bulkers has been linked to an order for six ultramax newbuildings at China’s Nantong Xiangyu Shipbuilding, marking its largest shipbuilding commitment since becoming a standalone company in 2021. articles.body: UPS reported higher third-quarter revenue across its domestic, international and supply chain businesses. Operating profit reached US$1.7 billion, while adjusted operating profit was US$2.1 billion. UPS reported diluted earnings of US$1.37 per share. Adjusted diluted earnings stood at US$1.69 per share. International revenue increased by 7.1% to slightly above US$5 billion. Revenue per piece rose by 15%, while operating profit reached US$746 million. The International segment achieved an operating margin of 14.9% on both a reported and adjusted basis. Forwarding and logistics support supply chain growth Supply Chain Solutions revenue increased by 18.2% to US$2.98 billion. UPS attributed the growth mainly to its forwarding and logistics operations, including healthcare logistics. Reported operating profit declined to US$92 million. It maintained its expectations for capital expenditure of US$3 billion and dividend payments of around US$5.4 billion, subject to board approval.

articles.body: Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, welcomed more than 5.38 million cruise passengers during fiscal year 2026, setting a new annual record for the third consecutive year. The latest figures reflect continued growth in the port’s cruise operations as it prepares for another season with additional vessels, upgraded facilities and expanded passenger services. The port expects to host nine cruise lines and 40 cruise ships during the new season. Participating operators include Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises, Disney Cruise Line, Princess Cruises, Holland America Line, Cunard, Crystal, Viking Ocean Cruises and Orient Express Sailing Yachts. The upcoming schedule also includes several new additions to the port’s homeporting operations. Royal Caribbean’s Legend of the Seas , an Icon-class cruise ship with capacity for up to 7,600 guests, is scheduled to arrive in November and homeport at Port Everglades for the 2027 season. Meanwhile, the newbuild Orient Express Corinthian will join the port’s cruise programme, alongside Crystal’s refurbished Crystal Symphony , which accommodates 606 guests. Port Everglades upgrades cruise infrastructure Alongside its passenger growth, Port Everglades has completed improvements to Cruise Terminal 18, which originally opened in 2009. The terminal has received a refreshed exterior, redesigned embarkation areas and additional passenger facilities. Improvements include more open interior spaces, new furniture and updated artwork in the VIP lounge. The port has also expanded parking capacity near the terminal. More than 850 spaces have been added, bringing the total number of available parking spaces across its garages and parking areas to 6,386. These upgrades are intended to support passenger operations as cruise activity continues to expand. New leadership for cruise operations Port Everglades has also appointed Martin Jackson as Director of its newly established Cruise Services Division. Jackson previously served as Assistant Director of the Cruise Services Section and joined the port in January 2025. The appointment follows approval of the fiscal year 2027 budget by the Broward County Board of County Commissioners. According to Joseph Morris, CEO and Port Director of Port Everglades, the organisational changes are designed to maintain service standards while supporting future growth. “Operational consistency earns trust, both internally and with our guests and customers, while continuous improvement ensures we are always making progress and moving ideas, vision, and strategy forward,” said Martin Jackson, Director of the Cruise Services Division at Port Everglades. The port has also released its 2027–2028 Cruise Guide, outlining upcoming sailings and itineraries for the new season.

articles.title: US revises tariffs on Canadian goods ahead of October 30 changes
articles.summary: The United States has announced changes to its 50% tariffs on selected Canadian products, removing certain goods from the existing measures while adding new product categories. The modifications were introduced through a presidential proclamation signed on October 23, 2026, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of...
articles.body: The United States has announced changes to its 50% tariffs on selected Canadian products , removing certain goods from the existing measures while adding new product categories. The modifications were introduced through a presidential proclamation signed on October 23, 2026, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. They will take effect on October 30, changing the tariff treatment of a range of Canadian goods entering the US market. The latest measures amend tariffs introduced in July and subsequently modified in September, reflecting another adjustment to trade restrictions between the two countries. Changes to products covered by US tariffs Under the revised measures, several Canadian products will no longer be subject to the additional 50% Section 338 duties. The exemptions include certain plywood sheets, paper and paperboard products, packaging materials, and selected industrial machinery and refrigeration equipment. According to a trade update published by Expeditors, other affected products include certain seaweeds and algae, along with non-adhesive sheets, films and foils made from polypropylene. At the same time, the US administration is expanding the list of goods covered by the additional duties. More than 100 products are being added, including certain paints, soaps, artificial waxes, vinyl flooring, fiberboard, carpets and industrial materials. The changes affect specific tariff classifications rather than all products within these broader categories. For importers and logistics providers, the revised product coverage will require attention to the applicable Harmonized Tariff Schedule classifications when arranging shipments and customs clearance. New tariff rules take effect on October 30 The White House confirmed that the changes will apply to covered goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouses for consumption, from 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on October 30, 2026. The administration also clarified that the additional Section 338 tariffs apply to covered Canadian goods regardless of whether they qualify as originating goods under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Furthermore, the measures may apply in addition to duties imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. The presidential proclamation authorises US Customs and Border Protection to issue the instructions and regulatory guidance necessary to implement the changes. The latest adjustments follow earlier modifications to the Section 338 measures in September, as the US administration continues to revise the scope of tariffs affecting Canadian exports. For companies involved in cross-border trade, the October 30 implementation date marks another change in the customs treatment of selected Canadian products.

articles.body: VLCC transits climb at Hormuz; steady at Bab al-Mandab for second day in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 The Strait of Hormuz had six VLCC transits on Oct. 25, the most since Oct. 17, while the Bab al-Mandab Strait recorded one VLCC on both Oct. 24 and Oct. 25, S&P Global Commodities at Sea said in an Oct. 26 report. Hormuz traffic in total was steady at 17 ships on Oct. 24 and Oct. 25, while Bab al-Mandab transits jumped to 42 ships from 27 ships over the same period, according to the CAS report. The VLCC total for Hormuz on Oct. 25 was up from five on Oct. 24, CAS data showed. The outbound VLCC from the Persian Gulf was Monaco Prosperity, while inbound VLCCs were Bangladesh Prosperity, Ennie, Thailand Prosperity, West Loyalty and Bulgaria Prosperity, CAS said. The VLCCs that transited Bab al-Mandab were Della, heading northbound, on Oct. 25 and Karina, also moving northbound, on Oct. 24, according to CAS. US forces on Oct. 25 marked the export of at least 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer through Hormuz, with US Central Command commander Admiral Brad Cooper flying over the chokepoint in a US Army CH-47 Chinook, Central Command said on X. It noted that more than 3,000 commercial ships had successfully transited Hormuz with support from CENTCOM forces over the last six months. “Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people,” Cooper said. “We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry.” The comment came despite Iran launching its heaviest wave of attacks on merchant ships around Hormuz and in the wider region this month, with the International Maritime Organization recording 29 attacks during Oct. 1-22, exceeding all monthly tallies since March. On Oct. 26, the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported a tanker exiting Hormuz was disabled after being struck by an unknown projectile Oct. 23. No crew casualties or oil spills have been reported. Of the 16 VLCC crossings identified over Oct. 23-25, 10 were assessed as inbound and six outbound, CAS said. Inbound VLCC movements included five of South Korea’s Sinokor-operated ships, and the Saudi-linked Majra and Qasba. The VLCC Ennie moved into the Persian Gulf after last loading a cargo of Basrah Heavy crude in early October, and China-owned VLCC Indigo Ray also moved inbound, CAS said. Outbound transits included Sinokor-operated Romania Prosperity, UAE-linked Das and Al Faya, and Saudi-linked Kahla and Emerald Shine, CAS said. LPG tankers Over Oct. 23-25, five LPG tankers were observed crossing the Strait of Hormuz, including one outbound and four inbound transits, CAS said. The outbound ship was the Marshall Islands-flagged Very Large Gas Carrier Sheng Hai Long, which had been in the Persian Gulf since Aug. 21, CAS said. During its stay, the ship loaded LPG at Ras Laffan, Qatar, while operating without AIS visibility, then exited the strait in a dark transit before reappearing in the Arabian Sea on Oct. 24, CAS said. On Oct. 24, two LPG tankers entered the Gulf. One was UAE-linked Sweihan, which previously transferred cargo at Vadinar, India, and was last seen heading for Ruwais, UAE, for its next loading, CAS said. On Oct. 25, UAE-linked LPG tanker Delma was last seen berthed at Ras Laffan for loading, CAS said. articles.body: Russian Diesel Returns: A New Atlantic Trade Dynamic in Hellenic Shipping News 28/10/2026 A new market development for tankers could be shaping up, after the latest agreement between US and Russia, regarding diesel exports across the Atlantic. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the latest developments in US–Russian energy relations could mark another turning point for the product tanker market, as Washington’s decision to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel opens the door to renewed trade flows between two countries whose energy relationship has been severely restricted since 2022. According to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, the first diesel cargo of approximately 40,000 mt is scheduled to depart Russia’s Baltic coast on October 22, with Moscow targeting 300,000 mt of shipments to the US during October and a further 500,000 mt in November. Beyond the political significance, this development raises important questions regarding Atlantic product tanker demand, vessel availability and the potential redistribution of established trading patterns”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker According to Xclusiv, “interestingly, maritime trade in petroleum products between Russia and the US has diminished significantly following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but has never completely disappeared. On 2020 and 2021 the seaborne trade of oil products from Russia to USA was around 23 million mt annually. Based on Signal Ocean data, during 2023, recorded shipments reached approximately 1.33 million mt, declining to 1.06 million mt in 2024, before recovering to 1.28 million mt in 2025. During January–June 2026, volumes totalled 510,000 mt, compared to 727,000 mt during the corresponding period of 2025, representing a contraction of almost 30%. July recorded no shipments, highlighting the weakening momentum before the latest diplomatic developments. These figures suggest that the announced reopening should be viewed not simply as the restoration of previously interrupted trade, but as a potential expansion and restructuring of existing flows, particularly concerning diesel”. The shipbroker added that “from a shipping perspective, the implications could be particularly interesting for the MR segment. The initial 40,000 mt cargo fits comfortably within MR2 employment, while the proposed 500,000 mt November programme could theoretically generate around 10–13 MR-sized cargoes, depending on parcel sizes. More importantly, shipments from Russia’s Baltic terminals towards the US Atlantic coast would introduce additional employment opportunities into a market already experiencing significant volatility. However, the actual benefit will depend on whether these shipments represent genuinely additional demand or simply replace diesel currently sourced from Northwest Europe, Canada and South Korea. In the latter case, the redistribution of existing cargoes could still reshape vessel positioning and regional freight differentials. Another important consideration is the current competition between clean and dirty tanker markets. With crude tanker earnings remaining exceptionally attractive, several LR vessels have shifted towards crude transportation, reducing the effective availability of tonnage dedicated to refined products. Returning these vessels to clean trading is neither immediate nor straightforward, as tank cleaning and preparation require additional time and costs. Consequently, renewed Russian diesel movements could arrive at a particularly favourable moment for MR owners, especially if increased Atlantic demand coincides with limited LR participation in the clean market”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker “Nevertheless, Russia’s ability to deliver the announced volumes remains uncertain. Ukrainian attacks against Russian refineries have constrained production and export capacity, while Moscow’s own restrictions on diesel exports underline the importance of protecting domestic supply. Although Novak anticipates a recovery towards the country’s traditional 3.5 million mt monthly diesel export capacity by year-end, actual shipments will depend heavily on refinery operations and logistical availability. Ultimately, the significance of this agreement extends beyond the initial cargoes. With gasoil prices remaining elevated and geopolitical disruptions continuing to reshape energy flows, even relatively modest changes in trade policy can influence vessel utilisation and freight sentiment. For product tanker owners, the key question is whether this reopening develops into a sustained Atlantic trade corridor. Should Russian export capacity recover while LR vessels remain attracted to the crude market, MR tankers could emerge as important beneficiaries of another geopolitical reshuffling of global petroleum trade”, Xclusiv concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Maritime industry advances harmonisation of digital emissions reporting
articles.summary: The Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group (JIWG) has released two new frameworks that can help improve the exchange of operations and emissions data across the maritime industry. The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and...
articles.body: Maritime industry advances harmonisation of digital emissions reporting in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 28/10/2026 T he Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group (JIWG) has released two new frameworks that can help improve the exchange of operations and emissions data across the maritime industry. The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and classification societies. As part of its work to develop a common approach for Maritime Emissions Reporting, the JIWG has released version 1.0 of the Operational Vessel Data (OVD) and Vessel Emissions Reporting (VER) frameworks. The two frameworks complement each other and can help establish a common foundation for a more efficient exchange of data. Both OVD and VER are voluntary industry frameworks. They do not create new reporting obligations but provide a common approach that organisations may adopt to support more efficient and consistent data exchange. The JIWG’s development of the OVD and VER frameworks complements and builds on earlier work by BIMCO and IACS (International Association of Classification Societies) to add emissions-reporting data elements to the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business. While the IMO Compendium provides common definitions and formats for maritime information, the latest work adds a practical implementation framework for exchanging operational vessel data and verified emissions-reporting results between industry systems. The initiative also forms part of a broader move towards using the IMO Compendium as a common foundation for maritime data exchange. Emerging use cases covering port-call optimisation, electronic seafarer certificates and maritime emissions reporting demonstrate how common data definitions can support interoperability across different parts of the maritime sector. The work of the group addresses the common industry challenge of stakeholders facing different reporting systems and data formats which often result in the same information being mapped, entered and checked multiple times. The OVD and VER can support a more consistent, efficient and traceable exchange of data between ships, shipping companies, software providers, verification bodies and other authorised users. The approach will also make it easier to reuse data more consistently across the industry and connected value chains. Two complementary parts of the data flow The OVD provides a structured format for exchanging operational vessel and fuel-consumption data. It defines common data elements, names, units and structures, allowing the information to be interpreted consistently by different systems and organisations. It does not prescribe how data must be collected onboard, which software must be used or where data must be stored, but instead provides a common approach for sharing such data across the maritime industry. The VER complements the OVD by providing standardised formats for emissions reporting in cases when commercial reporting practices and needs vary considerably. This could include charter-party performance, Emission Trading Schemes (ETS) cost allocation, FuelEU pooling and other commercial arrangements. The VER provides a common way to exchange emissions information, including its verification status for reporting periods that are defined by the user. In practical terms, the OVD provides the underlying operational data layer while the VER provides a structured output solution for emissions information. In combination, the two solutions can help support the maritime industry’s objective of capturing data only once and reusing it for all relevant reporting, verification and other purposes. See also the illustration in the annex, which shows the exchange of operational and emissions data across the maritime industry. Responding to a growing reporting burden The need for accurate and trusted maritime emissions reporting has increased due to the IMO Data Collection System (IMO DCS) and the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification system (EU MRV). Although these requirements serve different purposes, the use of different datasets and system formats can create inconsistencies, repeated data mapping and manual work across the reporting chain. The Tripartite JIWG has therefore worked to develop a common approach that allows data to move between different systems, regardless of the technology or service provider used. The OVD builds on a framework initially developed by DNV and subsequently considered through the wider JIWG process. The VER builds on an initial draft prepared by ClassNK and was further developed collaboratively by the participating organisations. Industry collaboration and practical implementation As voluntary industry frameworks, OVD and VER version 1.0 provides a baseline for practical use and further development. Organisations can now consider how the formats may be applied within existing systems and processes. Experience from implementation and real-world use will help identify where definitions, guidance, tools or data structures may need further refinement. Illustration of the exchange of operational and emissions data across the maritime As part of the next phase, the Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group will also assess options for transitioning OVD and VER towards independent and broadly representative governance. The objective is to establish clear ownership, open participation, transparent decision-making and predictable change management, providing confidence that the frameworks can be maintained as neutral and accessible industry resources. The Joint Industry Working Group will continue to oversee the work while the governance alternatives are assessed and until an appropriate structure is ready to receive the frameworks. No final governance model has yet been selected. Quotes Yasuhiro Ikeda, Director, Digital Solutions Division, ClassNK “VER is the result of a truly collaborative effort across all participating organisations, and I would like to thank everyone who contributed to this achievement. By establishing a common foundation for trusted and interoperable emissions data exchange, VER will help improve efficiency, transparency and digital collaboration across the maritime industry. Version 1.0 marks an important beginning, and we look forward to expanding its value through practical use and continued industry cooperation.” Bjarte Walaker, Head of Maritime Deliveries, Veracity by DNV “After several years of developing OVD, DNV is very pleased to see its broad adoption and grateful to the shipping companies, solution providers and other contributors who have helped turn it into a formal industry standard. This shared commitment is essential to enabling more efficient, consistent and interoperable exchange of vessel data, helping to reduce friction and support innovation across the maritime industry and connected value chains.” Vincent Joly, Smartship Manager – Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore “As reporting requirements continue to evolve, greater alignment in operational and emissions data is becoming increasingly important. Bureau Veritas has already adopted OVD for emissions data collection and supports this industry-led effort to establish common approaches for data exchange. These frameworks provide an important foundation for greater consistency across reporting and verification activities, enabling information to be shared and used more effectively across the maritime ecosystem.” Michela Schenone, Marine Digital and Class Solutions Operations Director – RINA “RINA believes that common industry standards are essential to make maritime emissions reporting more efficient, consistent and interoperable. RINA is taking practical steps to adopt OVD within its emissions reporting processes, supporting a common approach to data exchange across the industry. Continued industry collaboration will be key to achieving broad adoption and ensuring that these common frameworks deliver long-lasting value across the maritime sector.” Jeppe Skovbakke Juhl, Chief Naval Architect, Regulatory Affairs, BIMCO – chair of the JIWG “The maritime industry does not need more ways of exchanging the same information. It needs a common approach that allows data to move efficiently between organisations and systems. OVD and VER are an important step in that direction, reducing duplication and creating a stronger foundation for efficient and interoperable reporting.” Source: Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group Tops 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and classification societies.

As part of its work to develop a common approach for Maritime Emissions Reporting, the JIWG has released version 1.0 of the Operational Vessel Data (OVD) and Vessel Emissions Reporting (VER) frameworks.
The two frameworks complement each other and can help establish a common foundation for a more efficient exchange of data.

articles.summary: The International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI) has, today, released its 2026 analysis of the global marine insurance market – the IUMI “Stats Report”. articles.body: IUMI’s annual Stats Report highlights modest market development amid continued soft conditions across all main business lines in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 28/10/2026 T he International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI) has, today, released its 2026 analysis of the global marine insurance market – the IUMI “Stats Report”. This annual document reports on the state of the marine insurance sector within the framework of the global economy, trade and shipping. Data is collected from a wide range of national insurance associations and other agencies including IUMI’s own sources and is collated, analysed and presented with additional context and commentary. Highlights from this year’s report includes: • Global marine insurance premiums reached USD 42.6 billion in 2025, up 5.5 percent on 2024. However, US dollar weakness masked any underlying market development while increased capacity and competition continued to drive soft market conditions. • Marine cargo premiums were reported as USD 24.2 billion, up 6.9 percent year-on-year, supported by seaborne trade and asset and commodity price movements. Chinese premiums continued to grow strongly, driven by high-value exports including AI-related technology. Despite improving loss ratios, the market remained soft. • Ocean hull premiums increased 9.4 percent to USD 10.5 billion, encouraged by global fleet growth, higher vessel values and war premiums. Fleet growth continued to outpace premium growth indicating continued competitive pressure although loss ratios appear to have normalised. • Offshore energy premiums were broadly unchanged at USD 4.82 billion, up just 0.1 percent on 2024. London retained a 62.7 percent market share of which around 30% is renewables. While the market remains soft, energy security and geopolitical concerns could support significant future investment. As in previous years, the report also provides an update on IUMI’s Major Claims Database which contains data from 2013 onward with 30 national insurance associations now contributing. The number of observations for cargo claims has grown to 7,200 and a cumulative loss of USD 11.4 billion. IUMI’s revised Hull Inflation Index, which helps insurers to explain marine repair cost inflation using a range of macroeconomic indicators, is also showcased. Commenting on this year’s report, IUMI Secretary General, Lars Lange said: “The 2025 marine insurance market recorded modest growth in global premiums, although underlying conditions remained soft. Increased capacity, competitive pressures and currency movements, particularly the weakness of the US dollar, all influenced reported premium levels. On the claims side, the overall picture remained relatively stable with no single catastrophic loss significantly affecting any individual sector. However, attritional claims continued to accumulate putting pressure on profitability. Concerns that global tariffs would significantly constrain international trade proved less pronounced than anticipated while global GDP growth was stronger than expected. At the same time, the global race for AI began to influence marine trade with high-value semiconductors becoming an increasingly important component of international cargo movements. Asia continued to lead market growth with premium income rising steadily since 2016 and China remaining the region’s dominant market. European markets also expanded, although at a slower pace. Looking ahead, geopolitical tensions continued to shape the market into 2026. War cover became increasingly prominent while vessel availability, particularly for energy carriers, tightened as conflict in the Middle East intensified. Strong oil and gas demand continued to support activity while the impact of global tariffs remained less significant than initially feared. At IUMI, our job is to keep abreast of these many issues and engage with the relevant agencies to ensure marine underwriters are aware and equipped to continue to provide the insurance and risk mitigation services that ensure global trade continues without interruption. Our annual Stats Report is compiled by our Facts & Figures Committee together with input from a number of valued data partners. My thanks go to them all.” The full report is available to download from the statistics section of the IUMI website: https://iumi.com/statistics/iumi-stats-report-2026/ Source: IUMI Tops 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Tanker owners can’t call a $140m ship too old to upgrade, says BAR Technologies
articles.summary: With new VLCCs ordered today won’t be delivering until 2029, most of the ships that will carry the world’s oil this decade are already trading. Portsmouth, UK, 20 October 2026. articles.body: Tanker owners can’t call a $140m ship too old to upgrade, says BAR Technologies in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 With new VLCCs ordered today won’t be delivering until 2029, most of the ships that will carry the world’s oil this decade are already trading. Portsmouth, UK, 20 October 2026. With a 15-year-old tanker now worth more than a new one, owners have demolished their own favourite argument against retrofitting older ships, according to BAR Technologies CEO John Cooper. Poten & Partners values a VLCC available for prompt delivery at around $235 million, compared with approximately $130 million for a newbuilding ordered today and due for delivery in 2029. Even a 15-year-old VLCC could command around $140 million, according to the shipbroker. “The argument against retrofitting older ships has always been that it’s not worth spending money on a vessel near the end of its life,” said Cooper. “Well, the market has just put a $140 million price on a 15-year-old tanker. You can’t value a ship like that and then tell me it’s not worth improving.” Cooper expects many of those ships, some of which would have been heading for recycling within a few years, to keep trading into the 2030s. Every extra year is another year of fuel bills, and on a deep-sea ship, wind is, he says, “the only propulsion energy that’s free at source”. There is a regulatory argument, too. WindWings can reduce fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions, potentially improving a vessel’s Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rating and helping owners maintain its commercial viability as efficiency requirements tighten. For owners extending the working lives of older ships rather than replacing them, wind propulsion offers a way to improve operational performance while reducing fuel costs, strengthening the case for life extension, not just fuel savings. John Cooper, CEO of BAR Technologies BAR has modelled what that means for a VLCC on a typical USA to JPN trade. A typical 5x 37.5m WindWings® installation would save around 2670 tonnes of fuel a year (at a utilisation rate of 80%), worth $2.27m ($850/t assuming VLSFO usage) in saved fuel costs, paying back in 4 years based on fuel savings alone (without accounting for any carbon-related costs or benefits). [If confirmed: The work can be done during a routine dry-docking.] The technology is already working on existing ships. The bulk carriers Pyxis Ocean and Berge Olympus were both retrofitted with WindWings, and DNV independently recorded up to a 32% cut in main engine energy use on Pyxis Ocean in favourable conditions. Union Maritime has taken delivery of three WindWings-equipped LR2 tankers, with two more due in 2027. “Shipping has spent ten years telling itself that decarbonisation happens on the order book,” said Cooper. “The order book is full until 2029. The ships that have to burn less fuel this decade are the ones sailing now. “So if the market is comfortable putting $140 million on a 15-year-old tanker, owners should be asking themselves whether it still makes sense not to spend a fraction of that improving the way it runs.” Source: BAR Technologies 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
