articles.body: European Shipowners reiterate key asks for EU ETS negotiations in Council and Parliament in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 European shipping is a geopolitical asset for Europe, facilitating the export and import of goods, food and energy. While the EU represents around 15% of global GDP, the European fleet represents 34.5% of the world’s fleet in terms of global tonnage across all segments. As the European Parliament and the Council advance their work on the Commission proposal for the EU ETS revision, European Shipowners | ECSA highlight the key amendments needed for the revision to deliver on shipping’s energy transition while safeguarding the competitiveness of European shipping. A recent study found that shipping accounts for around 10% of EU ETS emissions but contributes almost 20% of ETS revenues. The new mechanism is an opportunity to reinvest part of this contribution in shipping’s energy transition. However, the 110 million allowances proposed by the Commission cover only a third of what is needed. We call on the policymakers to: • Reinvest ETS revenues in shipping’s decarbonisation. Shipping generates EUR 9 billion a year in national and EU ETS revenues. A recent study found that SMAP should be tripled from 110 million to 330 million allowances to help build a market for sustainable fuels and technologies. • Support all technologies. SMAP’s scope should be extended and cover all technologies that deliver carbon savings, including energy efficiency projects. • Make SMAP predictable. Predictability is essential: companies need certainty, before they take investment decisions, that the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels and technologies will be partly covered. Companies should be able to apply for support for fuels and technologies in advance. • Reward EU production. SMAP should incentivise the production of fuels and technologies in Europe through bonus points rather than made-in-Europe requirements. • Earmark a dedicated envelope for shipping. The general earmarking of Member States’ ETS revenues should include a specific percentage or envelope for shipping. • Apply one system to offshore vessels. The Commission has rightly recognised the need to change the rules applicable to offshore vessels, including the port call definition, to address unfair competition from non-EU offshore companies. However, applying one system from 2027 to 2030 and a different one from 2031 creates an unnecessary administrative burden. Only the new rules should apply. • Maintain, extend and improve derogations. Derogations for islands, outermost regions, ice-class vessels and transnational public services/obligations must be maintained, extended and made fit for purpose to support local economies, connectivity and regional cohesion. • Support port competitiveness without distorting competition. ES|ECSA shares the objective of keeping EU ports competitive. To maintain a level playing field across all shipping segments, the transhipment exemption should be replaced by an annual Commission report on port competitiveness and infrastructure needs. Where needed, national ETS revenues should support port infrastructure upgrades. • Simplify the EU MRV Regulation. Simplifying the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) Regulation is key to aligning the EU ETS, MRV and FuelEU Maritime, and to limiting the administrative burden on companies. “Shipping pays almost 20% of total ETS revenues, although it accounts for only 10% of the emissions covered by the system, and, unlike other sectors, it has never received a single free allowance. The European Parliament and the Council should at least triple the ETS revenues earmarked for SMAP to send a credible market signal for the scale-up of sustainable maritime fuels and technologies, including energy efficiency. Predictability is essential: companies need certainty, before they take investment decisions, that the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels will be partly covered. We strongly welcome the new provisions for offshore vessels. However, there is no justification for maintaining two consecutive and completely different reporting and compliance systems for these vessels. This significantly increases the administrative burden and undermines the competitiveness of the European offshore sector”, said Sotiris Raptis, Secretary General of European Shipowners | ECSA. Source: European Shipowners | ECSA 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 Singapore and Malaysia Bunker fuel availability remains tight in Singapore, with constrained fuel oil inventories. Reduced supply flows and tightening inventories across East of Suez continue to weigh on availability at the port. VLSFO lead times start at around 13 days at the earliest, and some suppliers recommend more than three weeks. Lead times were 12-15 days last week. HSFO lead times stand at around 10 days but stretch to as long as three weeks, almost unchanged from last week. LSMGO needs 9-11 days, compared with 7-14 days last week. Bunker supply in Port Klang, Malaysia, stays constrained across multiple grades. Prompt VLSFO availability is particularly tight, LSMGO supply is limited and HSFO availability faces continued pressure. East Asia VLSFO and HSFO availability remains tight in Zhoushan despite subdued demand, with several suppliers reporting low inventories and reduced imports, a source said. VLSFO lead times have shortened to eight days from 12 days last week, while HSFO lead times remain unchanged at 12 days. LSMGO availability has improved, with lead times falling to around four days from 12 days a week earlier. Bunker operations across Zhoushan have been suspended since last week due to rough weather brought by Typhoon Champi, the source said. The more sheltered Xiushandong briefly resumed operations yesterday before suspending them again. Operations could resume on 28 October as weather conditions are expected to improve. Supply conditions vary across other Chinese ports. Dalian and Qingdao have sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability remains tight in Qingdao. Tianjin is facing shortages across all three major fuel grades, while VLSFO and HSFO supplies are limited in Shanghai. LSMGO availability in Shanghai remains relatively stable. Supply constraints also persist in southern China, with suppliers in Fuzhou, Xiamen, Yangpu and Guangzhou reporting shortages of VLSFO and LSMGO. Hong Kong’s bunker market remains stable, with suppliers recommending lead times of around seven days for the major fuel grades. In Taiwan, VLSFO and LSMGO deliveries are available within two days at Keelung. Lead times are slightly longer at Hualien, Kaohsiung and Taichung, at around three days, largely unchanged from the previous week. Bunker demand has softened across South Korea as rising Brent futures have pushed benchmark prices higher. Busan’s VLSFO price has climbed by around $100/mt since the beginning of October to approximately $1,069/mt, according to a South Korean trader. At southern ports, including Busan, Ulsan, Masan, Onsan, Yeosu and Kwangyang, lead times for all major fuel grades have increased to around 5–8 days from 3–6 days a week earlier. In contrast, availability has improved at western ports, including Incheon, Daesan, Dangjin, Pyeongtaek and Taean. Lead times for VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO at these ports have fallen to 5–8 days from around 15 days previously. Adverse weather could disrupt bunker operations at several South Korean ports in the coming days. Busan and Ulsan may face interruptions on 28 October, 30–31 October and 1–4 November. Operations at Yeosu could be affected from 30 October to 1 November, while Daesan may experience disruptions between 27 October-1 November. VLSFO and HSFO availability remains severely constrained at several Japanese ports, including Tokyo, Chiba, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Yokkaichi, Osaka, Kobe, Mizushima, Tokuyama and Oita, where VLSFO stocks are nearly depleted. Most offers are subject to enquiry, and VLSFO is available only through spot offers in Tokyo, Chiba and Kawasaki. Term slots have been cancelled at these ports. Kashima is also experiencing tight availability of VLSFO and HSFO. Oceania Bunker fuel supply remains stable in Western Australia, with VLSFO readily available at Kwinana and Fremantle. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around seven days. Each port has only one supplier, and all bunker deliveries are made by barge. Supply conditions are mixed along Australia’s east coast. Port Kembla has normal VLSFO availability, with deliveries possible by truck or pipeline. Sydney has sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability is tighter, with suppliers generally requiring around seven days’ notice. Brisbane and Gladstone have ample supplies of VLSFO and LSMGO, with lead times of approximately one week. In contrast, VLSFO availability has tightened in Melbourne and Geelong, where one supplier has reported that stocks are nearly depleted. The supplier is awaiting replenishment cargoes, with constraints expected to persist until the first week of November. HSFO availability has also tightened further in Melbourne and Brisbane. The approaching cyclone season could pose additional risks to bunker operations across Australia, a source said. Running from November to April, the season could disrupt fuel availability at ports nationwide. New Zealand’s bunker market remains broadly stable, with VLSFO readily available at Tauranga and Auckland. Suppliers at both ports are recommending lead times of around four days. At Marsden Point, vessels can receive VLSFO and LSMGO directly through the pipeline. Adverse weather remains the main operational risk in New Zealand, particularly in Wellington and ports across the South Island, where disruptions to marine operations could delay bunker deliveries. In Papua New Guinea, bunker fuel availability remains tight across all major grades at the ports of Rabaul and Lae. South Asia Weather-related disruptions are expected at India’s Visakhapatnam port from 27–31 October, potentially delaying bunker operations. Very severe cyclonic storm Arnab was located about 140 km from Kakinada and 170 km from Visakhapatnam at noon on Tuesday, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The storm is expected to cross the coast just south of Yanam by Wednesday forenoon, bringing winds of 125–135 kmph and gusts of up to 150 kmph. A storm surge of 1–2 metres could inundate low-lying areas near Kakinada and Yanam. The intensifying cyclone is moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, prompting storm warnings at several ports. Kakinada Port has been placed under the highest-level warning, while Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram, Machilipatnam and Nizampatnam ports have received high-level maritime storm warnings. articles.title: New Report Exposes Critical Need For Trusted Digital Seafarer Credentials
articles.summary: A comprehensive new report entitled Securing Trust: The Transition to Digital Seafarer Credentials, published by maritime technology research firm Thetius in partnership with Maritime Passport, reveals that the global shipping industry’s reliance on paper certificates and disconnected digital copies poses significant...
articles.body: New Report Exposes Critical Need For Trusted Digital Seafarer Credentials in International Shipping News 28/10/2026 A comprehensive new report entitled Securing Trust: The Transition to Digital Seafarer Credentials, published by maritime technology research firm Thetius in partnership with Maritime Passport, reveals that the global shipping industry’s reliance on paper certificates and disconnected digital copies poses significant operational, security, and administrative risks. With an estimated 2.57 million seafarers serving on more than 85,000 merchant ships worldwide, maritime professionals are still routinely required to carry physical copies of certificates weighing up to four kilograms. The report emphasises that simply converting physical documents into unstructured electronic PDFs or disconnected digital portals cannot solve the industry’s verification challenge. Rather, there is a need for a globally trusted, interoperable trust framework that offers high levels of security but does not create more work for the various stakeholders – especially seafarers. Front cover of Thetius/Maritime Passport report Photo credit: Thetius “As an ex-seafarer myself, I have long been advocating for greater use of digital technologies in ways that benefit seafarers, and this report highlights the ways in which digital verification can and must evolve. But it’s vital that we do this correctly,” explains Martin White, Co-Founder of Maritime Passport. “Remarkable advances in digital identity, biometrics and secure credential technologies make a transition to digital verification possible, but they also raise important questions around legitimacy, governance, interoperability and adoption. Interoperability is essential, but it must strengthen these principles, never compromise them.” “In a digital age, trust both in technology but also in chosen partners, is non-negotiable,” explains Peter Phillips, Co-Founder of Maritime Passport. “Moving from paper to digital means protecting a seafarer’s identity, qualifications, and ultimately their livelihood, while safeguarding highly sensitive personal information. Digital credentials must reinforce issuing authority while giving employers, inspectors, and other key stakeholders confidence that every credential is valid, up to date, and held by the rightful individual.” Key findings of the Report Heavy administrative burden: Verifying credentials for a single seafarer can take between one and two hours for crewing recruitment teams. A recent industry survey cited in the report found that port call document preparation averages 191 minutes, with 64% of port calls still relying on paper or mixed paper/digital submissions. Operational delays and livelihood risks: Physical certificates and sea service records remain highly vulnerable to loss or damage. Replacing lost paper credentials requires contacting multiple issuing authorities, during which time a seafarer is unable to work, leading to crew change disruptions and vessel delays. Security and fraud vulnerabilities: With thousands of training institutions and national formats worldwide, visual inspection of certificates is increasingly unreliable. Forged or fraudulently altered certificates, as well as revoked or expired credentials remaining in circulation, continue to pose safety and regulatory compliance risks. Scanned copies and PDFs do not fix this: credentials need to be linked to verified digital identities that can be checked independently. Data protection and privacy risks: Scanned copies of passports and personal qualification records are frequently emailed and stored indefinitely on vessel computers and company servers, creating significant data privacy and GDPR compliance risks. Accelerating regulatory momentum: Recent amendments to the STCW Convention (effective January 2025) officially define “original form” to include electronic formats. Additionally, the IMO Strategy on Maritime Digitalisation approved at FAL 50 underlines an urgent industry shift toward standardised, interoperable digital data exchange. Other findings from the report include the need to preserve the authority of credential issuers rather than build a single global platform, the operational benefits of verified credentials for crew changes, inspections and crewing teams, and the importance of cyber resilience and offline verification. Recommendations for industry adoption: Establish Common Rules: International bodies and flag states must agree on baseline standards for digital credential validity, verification, data protection, and dispute handling. Design for a Phased Transition: System must support paper, digital copies, and native digital credentials simultaneously as maritime organisations transition at different speeds. Prioritise Interoperability: Buyers and regulators should mandate open standards and exit capabilities to prevent vendor lock-in and isolated digital silos. Support Developing Nations: Infrastructure solutions must accommodate smaller or lower-resource administrations to prevent a digital divide within the seafaring workforce. Source: Thetius and Maritime Passport 2026-10-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

The report emphasises that simply converting physical documents into unstructured electronic PDFs or disconnected digital portals cannot solve the industry’s verification challenge.

articles.body: Seven Japanese Companies Jointly Announce to Build and Operate Four Ammonia-Fueled Car Carriers and Commercialize the Ammonia Bunkering Business in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 28/10/2026 Imabari Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. (“Imabari Shipbuilding”), Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, Ltd. (““K” LINE”), Kyokuyo Shipyard Corporation (“Kyokuyo Shipyard”), JERA Co., Inc. (“JERA”), Shin Kurushima Dockyard Co., Ltd. (“Shin Kurushima Dockyard”), Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (“NYK”), and Nihon Shipyard Co., Ltd. (“NSY”), jointly announced that they have agreed to develop an ammonia fuel supply chain in Japan’s Chubu region and to build and operate four ammonia-fueled car carriers supported by the supply chain. Purpose and Overview of the Project This project will be a comprehensive initiative to develop an integrated ammonia fuel supply chain, from the procurement of green ammonia and development of ship loading facilities to the construction of a dedicated bunkering vessel* with fuel supply through ship-to-ship (STS) bunkering,** and the operation of ammonia-fueled car carriers. To address the need to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping as well as customers’ Scope 3 emissions, the seven companies aim to establish a stable ammonia fuel supply system through the integrated development of the supply chain. This project will be the world’s first commercial supply chain, with the Chubu region serving as the hub, integrating fuel procurement, supply infrastructure at the Hekinan terminal, and vessel operations. Ammonia is a next generation fuel that emits no carbon dioxide (CO₂) when combusted and can be stored and transported in liquid form. In particular, steady progress is being made toward the practical use of low-carbon ammonia, which is produced with reduced CO₂ emissions during the manufacturing process, in the power generation sector. In the future, its use is also expected to expand into the transport sector, including maritime applications and other industries. By combining their respective technologies, expertise, and infrastructure, the seven companies will establish an advanced integrated business model that brings together ammonia fuel procurement and supply, the construction of ammonia-fueled car carriers, and development of an ammonia bunkering vessel. Through this initiative, the companies will promote the decarbonization of international shipping through a Japanese industry collaboration while also supporting the broader utilization of ammonia for industrial and other applications. In doing so, they aim to contribute to the realization of a sustainable society and the development of a low-carbon ammonia market. Fuel Procurement and Development of Ship Loading Facilities (JERA) JERA is advancing the development of a lower-carbon ammonia value chain as part of its efforts to achieving net-zero CO₂ emissions from its domestic and overseas businesses by 2050, and contribute to global decarbonization and address the world’s energy issues. Its initiatives include the use of lower-carbon ammonia at the Hekinan Thermal Power Station for fuel substitution to decarbonize the thermal power generation business, and the installation of tank truck loading facilities to supply lower-carbon ammonia to other businesses. Under this project, JERA will procure green ammonia produced using renewable energy. These supplies are intended to come from regions including India. In addition, JERA will develop new ship loading facilities at the ammonia receiving terminal adjacent to the Hekinan Thermal Power Station, which will establish a stable supply system for the bunkering vessel. JERA will contribute significantly to the decarbonization of international shipping and to Japan’s decarbonization efforts, with the Chubu region serving as a key hub. Building of Ammonia Bunkering Vessel and Fuel Supply and Sales Structure (“K” LINE, Kyokuyo Shipyard, and NYK) Kyokuyo Shipyard, which possesses advanced technical capabilities in building specialized vessels, will build the ammonia bunkering vessel. It is scheduled for completion in 2030, the same as ammonia-fueled car carriers. Following completion, the vessel will be owned and operated by NYK or a wholly owned NYK subsidiary. “K” LINE and NYK will also establish a fuel sales joint venture, equally owned by the two companies, to facilitate fuel sales and supply between vessels. Using a bunkering vessel owned and operated by NYK or a wholly owned NYK subsidiary, the joint venture will supply ammonia fuel to car carriers through STS bunkering. By combining the stringent safety standards and operational expertise the two companies have accumulated in handling ammonia and LNG, they aim to establish a safe, highly efficient fuel supply system. Building and Operation of Four Ammonia-Fueled Car Carriers (Imabari Shipbuilding, “K” LINE, Shin Kurushima Dockyard, NYK, and NSY) “K” LINE and NYK are working to transition to next-generation fuels to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and provide cleaner transportation services that meet society’s growing need for low-carbon and decarbonized solutions. Under this project, each company will introduce two ammonia-fueled car carriers, for a total of four vessels. Following their scheduled completion in 2030, the vessels are expected to transport finished vehicles for customers including Toyota Motor Corporation. The vessels will be Japan’s first ammonia-fueled car carriers. They will be equipped with dual-fuel engines capable of using ammonia as fuel, as well as fuel tanks with sufficient capacity to enable trans-Pacific voyages using ammonia fuel alone. To ensure the safe use of ammonia, which is toxic and corrosive, the vessels will also incorporate a multilayered safety concept, including measures to prevent and detect leaks and to neutralize ammonia in the event of a leak. Drawing on the world’s most extensive track record in building car carriers, Shin Kurushima Dockyard will lead the basic design phase. The vessels will then be jointly designed and built by Shin Kurushima Dockyard, Imabari Shipbuilding, and NSY — each bringing deep, proven expertise in car-carrier construction. By bringing together their advanced technological and shipbuilding capabilities, the three companies aim to realize next-generation vessels that combine high safety in open-sea operations with world-leading environmental performance, thereby demonstrating the competitiveness of Japan’s shipbuilding technologies on the global stage. articles.title: Q&A: Shipfinex CEO shares his thoughts on widening access to vessel investment
articles.summary: Capt. Vikas Pandey, Founder and CEO of Shipfinex, shares his thoughts on widening access to vessel investment, new funding opportunities for shipowners and the risks investors should understand in this Q&A. How traditional ship ownership is changing, and what the market could look like once a much wider pool of...
articles.body: Capt. Vikas Pandey, Founder and CEO of Shipfinex, shares his thoughts on widening access to vessel investment, new funding opportunities for shipowners and the risks investors should understand in this Q&A. How traditional ship ownership is changing, and what the market could look like once a much wider pool of investors can gain exposure to the ships moving global trade. For most of shipping’s history, ownership sat with families, a handful of funds and banks. A vessel was a single, indivisible asset worth tens of millions, so the investor pool was naturally small. That is starting to change. Tokenisation lets ownership of an individual vessel be divided into smaller units, held by a much wider and more global pool of investors, with ownership records and earnings distributions handled transparently on-chain. As that pool widens, I expect three things: Owners will treat capital raising as a continuous process rather than a once-a-cycle event. Pricing of individual assets will become more transparent, because more participants will be valuing the same ship. The line between public shipping equities and private vessel ownership will blur, with investors choosing exposure to a specific ship, segment or charter profile rather than a whole company. Whether opening vessel financing to smaller investors could bring shipowners a new source of capital. Yes, and it matters most for small and mid-sized owners. Bank lending to shipping has contracted over the past decade and remains concentrated on the largest names. Private credit is filling part of the gap, but at a cost. A broader investor base gives owners another source of equity, tied to the asset rather than requiring a public listing of the whole company. What investors need to understand about vessel earnings, costs and their ability to exit. Investors need to understand that a ship is an operating business, not a passive asset. On earnings: a vessel on a long-term time charter behaves very differently from one trading on the spot market. One gives more predictable income; the other gives upside with real volatility. Investors should know the charter, the counterparty and when it expires. On costs: operating expenses, drydocking, survey cycles, insurance and crew costs all come before any distribution. A five-yearly special survey can absorb a significant share of a year’s earnings. Age and condition of the vessel matter enormously. On structure: investors should know exactly what they hold. Is it economic rights, equity in a vessel-owning SPV, or a debt instrument? Who has priority? In ship finance, a first-priority registered ship mortgage generally ranks ahead of equity holders, and investors need to see that clearly. On exit: liquidity is not automatic. A digital token does not create buyers by itself. Investors should ask whether there is a regulated secondary market, what the lock-ins are, and what happens at the end of the vessel’s life, whether through sale or recycling. The opportunity is real, but it only works if disclosure is as rigorous as the technology.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is calling on the U.S. Coast Guard to establish national safety standards for uncrewed surface vessels after an investigation found that a NOAA research vessel was difficult to detect and lacked adequate monitoring when it collided with a recreational boat on Lake Erie. In findings released Tuesday, the NTSB issued six safety recommendations addressing vessel visibility, collision avoidance, and remote monitoring, highlighting regulatory gaps as uncrewed and autonomous vessels become increasingly common in U.S. waters. The investigation stems from an August 10, 2024, collision between a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) SeaTrac SP-48 uncrewed surface vessel and a privately owned 45-foot Prestige 450 Flybridge recreational boat approximately six miles east-southeast of Monroe, Michigan. The 15.7-foot research vessel became entangled in the recreational boat’s starboard propeller pod, leaving the two vessels stuck together. Both were towed to a nearby marina and later separated. One minor injury was reported. The NOAA vessel was declared a constructive total loss, valued at approximately $186,000, while damage to the recreational boat was estimated at $100,000. According to the NTSB investigation report, the uncrewed vessel’s low-profile design made it particularly difficult for other mariners to see. Only about one foot of its hull was visible above the water, and investigators determined it was unlikely to be detected by the radar or automatic identification systems typically used aboard recreational vessels in the area. The vessel also lacked an audible means of warning approaching traffic. But visibility was only part of the problem. At the time of the collision, NOAA’s Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory was operating the vessel in an automated station-keeping configuration known as “adapted hold” mode. The system allowed the vessel to return automatically to preset waypoints whenever it drifted beyond a 150-foot radius. A remote pilot monitored the vessel from shore, but the NTSB found that the monitoring was passive and insufficient for the operating conditions. Critically, the vessel lacked the autonomy needed to independently assess nearby traffic and take collision-avoidance action. Investigators concluded that the combination of poor visibility and inadequate monitoring effectively left the vessel without a proper lookout. “The USV could not calculate decisions regarding navigation or operational action and thus could not take appropriate action to avoid a collision,” the NTSB said. The findings raise broader questions about how remotely operated vessels should comply with established navigation safety requirements, particularly when operating alongside conventional vessels in busy waterways. Coast Guard Urged to Establish National Standards The investigation found that, at the time of the collision, there were no industry-wide standards specifically addressing the perceptibility, collision-avoidance capabilities, and navigational safety of uncrewed surface vessels operating in U.S. inland and territorial waters. The NTSB is now recommending that the Coast Guard develop a national framework covering those areas and incorporate the standards into federal regulations. “As USVs become more commonplace in U.S. waterways, it is critical for the Coast Guard to begin to set standards and policies for these vessels,” the report said. The agency also issued three recommendations to NOAA, calling for revisions to its internal operating procedures to ensure its uncrewed vessels can be adequately detected by other mariners. Those changes would include testing vessels against the types of traffic they are likely to encounter and requiring remote monitoring appropriate to each vessel’s actual level of autonomy, operating environment, and mode of operation. Manufacturer SeaTrac Systems Inc. was separately urged to modify the SP-48’s design to improve its visibility and detectability. The recommendations come as the maritime industry increasingly adopts uncrewed vessels for oceanographic research, hydrographic surveying, environmental monitoring, and other operations. The NTSB’s recommendations do not themselves establish new regulations, but they put additional pressure on the Coast Guard to address those questions as uncrewed vessel operations expand. articles.body: DP World has appointed Amer Abdulrahim Kazim and Iman Al Qasim as Independent Non-Executive Directors to its Board, effective immediately. The global ports and logistics operator announced the appointments on October 26, 2026. Both executives bring extensive experience in finance, corporate governance, human capital and organisational transformation. According to DP World, the appointments will strengthen the Board’s expertise and support the company’s long-term strategic objectives. New directors bring financial and leadership experience Amer Abdulrahim Kazim currently serves as Group Chief Audit Officer at Emirates NBD Group. He has more than 27 years of experience across banking, aviation, telecommunications and real estate. Previously, Kazim served as Chief Financial Officer at Emirates Integrated Telecommunications Company (du). He also held senior positions at Emirates Group, Meraas and Dubai Airports. She brings more than 20 years of experience in human capital management and organisational transformation. Her previous leadership positions include roles at Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC), Mubadala Investment Company, Dolphin Energy and General Motors Middle East. Al Qasim also serves on the Board of Directors of E7 Group. DP World strengthens corporate governance The appointments add expertise in financial oversight, organisational development and corporate management to DP World’s Board. Essa Kazim, Group Executive Chairman of DP World, welcomed both executives and highlighted their professional backgrounds. “I am pleased to welcome Mr Kazim and Ms Al Qasim to the Board,” said Essa Kazim, Group Executive Chairman of DP World. “Their extensive experience and expertise across a range of industries will bring valuable perspectives to DP World as we continue to strengthen our governance and deliver on our long-term strategic objectives,” he added. articles.title: Russia Says Northern Sea Route Transit Cargo to Nearly Double in 2026
articles.summary: Russia expects cargo transits along the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to more than double in 2026, marking a substantial increase in Arctic shipping despite Western sanctions, although volumes remain far below Moscow’s original ambitions for the route.

(Source: Atomflot via Telegram) Russia expects cargo transits along the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to more than double in 2026, marking a substantial increase in Arctic shipping despite Western sanctions, although volumes remain far below Moscow’s original ambitions for the route. Transit cargo will exceed 7 million tonnes this year, Vladimir Panov, head of the Arctic Directorate at state nuclear corporation Rosatom, said on Oct. 27. Total cargo traffic along the route is expected to surpass 40 million tonnes, also a record, he said. “The Northern Sea Route has two competitive advantages – efficiency and security,” Panov said, adding that the summer-fall route between Asia and Europe is 30% shorter than the passage through the Suez Canal. “Businesses are already voting for the NSR with tonnes,” he said. Transit cargo, which excludes commodities extracted in the Russian Arctic, is a small but growing component of overall traffic. Russia’s forecast of more than 7 million tonnes would nearly double the previous year’s volume, Panov said. Independent tracking by Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) offers a more conservative assessment. By Sept. 30, researchers had identified 104 confirmed transits, already exceeding the 103 recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season. Estimated cargo carried stood at 3.7 million tonnes, compared with 3.2 million tonnes for all of 2025. CHNL estimated that the season could approach 150 transits and exceed 4.5 million tonnes of cargo if most of the voyages already underway at the end of September were completed. The organization’s figures are preliminary estimates based on vessel tracking and available cargo information, rather than official statistics. Oil shipments have been a major driver of this year’s surge. In an unprecedented Arctic operation in August, a convoy of at least 15 vessels, including eight oil tankers, sailed north of the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago to bypass difficult ice conditions in the Vilkitsky Strait . The detour took the ships above 81.5 degrees north, along a route nearly 1,000 kilometers longer than the conventional passage. Russian oil shipments through the NSR had reached approximately 20 million barrels between the start of navigation in July and mid-October, nearly 50% above the previous year’s total. The longer-term picture is equally striking. Total NSR cargo traffic has risen from about 3.7 million tonnes in 2014 to more than 37 million tonnes in each of the past two years, driven overwhelmingly by Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other resource exports. Yet the growth has fallen well short of the Kremlin’s original targets. President Vladimir Putin had set an 80-million-tonne goal for 2024, before later projecting that annual traffic could reach 70 million to 100 million tonnes by 2030. Russia carried approximately 38 million tonnes in 2024. Western sanctions have delayed or complicated several major Arctic oil and gas developments, limiting the expansion of cargo volumes. Nevertheless, the latest figures demonstrate that Moscow continues to develop the route and redirect trade toward Asian markets, albeit at a slower pace than originally envisioned. It also increasingly relies on sanctioned or shadow fleet vessels to carry goods across the Arctic. Further growth could come from Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project, a major planned oil development on Russia’s Taymyr Peninsula. Increased crude shipments through the Arctic could add substantially to traffic if production and export infrastructure ramp up as planned. Novatek’s LNG exports could also contribute to the shift. The European Union’s planned prohibition on Russian LNG imports under its phaseout schedule, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, is likely to increase pressure on Russian producers to find alternative markets in Asia. The extent to which this translates into additional NSR shipments will depend on production, shipping capacity, ice conditions and available receiving infrastructure. Container shipping is also expanding , although it remains a small part of the route’s overall business. Panov said the number of transit container voyages would rise to 46 this year from 23 in 2025, with international containerized transit cargo expected to exceed 600,000 tonnes. However, those figures have not been independently verified and sit well above what the CHNL observed, which reported just 13 voyages by the end of September. The NSR remains primarily an export corridor for Russian Arctic resources rather than a major alternative to established global shipping lanes. This year’s record figures nevertheless show that sanctions have not halted Russia’s Arctic ambitions. articles.body: Damen Shipyards Group has placed a new order with EST-Floattech for two additional Octopus Series battery systems. The systems will be installed on two Damen Combi Freighter (CF) 3850 cargo vessels. Announced on October 26, the agreement extends the companies’ existing cooperation on battery technology for short-sea shipping. It also renews their framework agreement, which followed a partnership established in November 2024. With the latest order, the total number of EST-Floattech battery systems installed or planned for installation on CF 3850 vessels will reach nine. The collaboration focuses on improving vessel efficiency and supporting the transition towards lower-emission shipping operations. Damen expands battery integration across cargo vessels The CF 3850 is a cargo vessel designed for short-sea shipping markets. According to Damen, the next-generation version has attracted 50 orders over the past five years. The vessel features an optimised hull design and can accommodate various energy-saving technologies. These options allow operators to improve efficiency while adapting the vessel to their operational requirements. Among the available solutions is the EST-Floattech Octopus battery system. Its capacity ranges from 240 kWh to 1,320 kWh, depending on the configuration selected by the operator. The system can support several onboard functions, including peak shaving and bow thruster operations. Depending on the installed capacity, it can also enable port calls without emissions from onboard power generation during battery-powered operations. By integrating battery storage, vessel operators can reduce reliance on conventional generators during selected operating conditions. “The CF 3850 is a proven vessel with an extensive track record,” said Arjan de Vries, Manager Procurements at Damen Cargo Vessels. De Vries explained that Damen aims to combine its established vessel platform with reliable technologies. He also highlighted the flexibility of the Octopus system, which can be scaled to meet different customer requirements. EST-Floattech strengthens cooperation with Damen The latest order continues a partnership focused on integrating battery storage into commercial cargo vessels. For EST-Floattech, repeated installations on the same vessel design provide opportunities to evaluate system performance and improve future configurations. “We were very pleased to receive this latest order from Damen Cargo Vessels,” said Jelle Meindertsma, Sales Manager at EST-Floattech. Meindertsma highlighted the companies’ ongoing cooperation and the benefits of applying battery technology to an established vessel platform. The Octopus Series is designed to provide modular energy storage solutions for maritime applications. Its flexible configuration allows operators to select battery capacity according to their operational needs. Meanwhile, Damen continues to offer battery integration as part of its wider range of efficiency improvements for the CF 3850. The companies have not disclosed the financial value of the latest order or the specific battery capacities selected for the two vessels. They have also not announced an installation or delivery schedule. Nevertheless, the agreement increases the number of CF 3850 vessels equipped or scheduled to be equipped with EST-Floattech technology, extending the companies’ cooperation in short-sea shipping.

The systems will be installed on two Damen Combi Freighter (CF) 3850 cargo vessels.

Photo courtesy Georgia Ports The Trump administration announced $498 million in federal grants Tuesday to modernize U.S. ports, funding 35 projects across 19 states ranging from aging dock replacements and cargo-handling equipment to fuel terminal upgrades and advanced maritime monitoring systems. The funding, awarded through the Maritime Administration’s (MARAD) Port Infrastructure Development Program (PIDP), is aimed at improving cargo movement, expanding capacity and strengthening supply chains at coastal seaports, Great Lakes facilities and inland river ports. While significant, the latest round is smaller than the grants awarded in each of the previous four fiscal years. MARAD awarded $774 million to 37 projects in fiscal year 2025, announced this past April, compared with approximately $580 million in 2024, $653 million in 2023 and $703 million in 2022. The new $498 million round is roughly 36% below last year’s total and 26% below the average awarded over the previous four fiscal years. Among the largest recipients is the City of Whittier, Alaska, which will receive $50.6 million to replace the DeLong Dock, install a seasonal floating dock and acquire three pedestal cranes along with an integrated tug and barge. Port Everglades in Florida will receive $30.75 million to strengthen its liquid bulk terminal, widen a slip to accommodate larger vessels and improve resilience to severe weather. The improvements are intended to help maintain critical fuel operations during storms. In North Carolina, the state ports authority will receive $11.25 million for upgrades at the Port of Morehead City, including new heavy-lift cargo infrastructure, crane rails and expanded on-dock rail connections. The project also includes security and cargo-tracking technology. The Red Wing Port Authority in Minnesota will receive $10.2 million to rebuild barge-loading infrastructure along the Mississippi River, including conveyors, an electric winch and dust collection systems. The project will also elevate critical equipment above the river’s floodplain. In Texas, Port Freeport will receive $9.4 million to replace an aging bulk rice loader and expand cargo-handling space, while the Port of Corpus Christi will receive $7.2 million to develop a digital twin of its infrastructure. The Corpus Christi project will incorporate LiDAR, sonar, cameras and other sensing technologies to provide continuous monitoring of port facilities and transportation connections. Smaller projects include nearly $699,000 for Rockport Harbor in Maine to construct a new commercial fishing pier designed to improve transfers of seafood from vessels to trucks. “The strength of our nation’s economy is directly tied to the state of our ports,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. “This nearly half-billion-dollar investment will deliver critical upgrades to ports across America so we can enhance supply chains, lower shipping costs, and create good-paying jobs for hardworking Americans.” MARAD Administrator Stephen Carmel described the awards as part of the administration’s broader maritime revitalization effort. “The President’s commitment to modernizing our port and maritime infrastructure has resulted in an unprecedented investment that will empower local port communities to modernize their operations, integrate innovative technologies, and create safer working environments,” Carmel said. The grants come as one of the federal government’s largest dedicated sources of port infrastructure funding approaches a transition. Much of the current funding stems from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law signed by President Joe Biden in 2021, which provided $2.25 billion for the PIDP over five years, including $450 million annually from fiscal 2022 through 2026. The Trump administration has proposed maintaining $500 million in PIDP funding for fiscal 2027, including $50 million through regular appropriations and another $450 million through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund, a central component of the administration’s maritime revitalization strategy. The investments come as the administration pursues its broader maritime dominance agenda, which includes expanding U.S. shipbuilding capacity, strengthening the merchant marine and modernizing maritime infrastructure. Photo: Villa Vie Residences Villa Vie Residences has suspended operations of its residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey in Cambodia, forcing residents to disembark as soaring fuel costs push the company toward financial restructuring. The Fort Lauderdale-based company announced Tuesday that it is evaluating restructuring and recapitalization options over the next 60 days after a sharp increase in fuel expenses made its current operating model financially unsustainable. According to the company, monthly fuel expenses on an equivalent per-cabin basis have surged from a historical average of approximately $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 in parts of Asia, an increase of as much as 344%. The company attributed the increases to the conflict with Iran, which began in late February and has disrupted energy markets and shipping operations worldwide. “Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs.” The financial pressures have brought an abrupt halt to a voyage that was marketed as a continuous, around-the-world residential cruise. In a notice to residents on Monday, October 26, Villa Vie CEO Kathy Villalba said the company had been unable to secure the fuel needed to continue operating. The vessel would enter temporary layup, with crew remaining aboard to maintain essential systems. Residents were instructed to leave the vessel by 2 p.m. that day, according to a copy of the notice published by resident Randy Cassingham . The company said it is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements, acknowledging the disruption for residents, crew members and employees. The shutdown follows earlier efforts to raise additional funding. Cruise Industry News reported that Villa Vie had sought financial contributions from residents, including a recent request for $360,000 to cover fuel expenses. In April, the company reportedly offered residents an emergency loan investment opportunity seeking $3 million, with interest rates ranging from 12% to 24%. It was unclear how much funding, if any, was raised. Cassingham, writing about the shutdown, said the company’s problems extended beyond fuel prices, citing a combination of weaknesses in the business model, management decisions and rising operating expenses. The 195-meter Villa Vie Odyssey , formerly Fred. Olsen Cruise Lines’ Braemar , was acquired by Villa Vie in March 2024 and underwent refurbishment in Belfast before beginning its continuous world voyage in October of that year. The company’s concept offered residents the opportunity to purchase cabins aboard the ship and travel indefinitely, with itineraries taking the vessel to hundreds of destinations around the world. Its Endless Horizons program also offered lifetime cruising through a one-time payment. The financial crisis comes just three months after Villa Vie announced plans for a second residential cruise ship , Legacy , which was expected to enter service in early 2029. At the time, the company said more than 85% of available residences aboard Odyssey had been sold. It also announced plans to extend lifetime residency rights to Legacy and introduced a program allowing new buyers to live aboard Odyssey before transferring to the second vessel. Tuesday’s announcement did not address the future of Legacy or how the suspension might affect residents who purchased cabins or lifetime cruising rights. Villa Vie said it continues to evaluate financing and restructuring alternatives, but no transaction has been finalized and there is no confirmed timetable for resuming operations. The company acknowledged that the outcome of its restructuring efforts remains uncertain. “No outcome is assured,” it said. articles.title: EVI introduces AI safety camera mode to protect seafarer privacy
articles.summary: EVI Safety Technology has launched Crew-First Mode, a new feature for its AI-powered onboard camera system. The technology aims to improve maritime safety while giving seafarers greater protection against routine remote monitoring. The new setting allows the system to detect potential safety risks and alert crew...
articles.body: EVI Safety Technology has launched Crew-First Mode, a new feature for its AI-powered onboard camera system. The technology aims to improve maritime safety while giving seafarers greater protection against routine remote monitoring. The new setting allows the system to detect potential safety risks and alert crew members. At the same time, it limits access to camera footage from shore-based teams. When Crew-First Mode is activated, shore personnel continue to receive safety notifications. However, the associated video footage remains onboard, and routine shore viewing is disabled. According to EVI, the approach allows crews to benefit from AI-assisted safety monitoring without automatically sharing visual records of their activities with shore offices. AI safety monitoring with limits on remote access EVI’s safety technology uses existing onboard cameras to identify potential hazards and notify crew members. This allows personnel to respond to detected risks during vessel operations. The introduction of Crew-First Mode adds another layer of control over how the system handles visual information. Rather than routinely transmitting alert footage to shore-based personnel, the new setting keeps that material onboard. Shore teams can still receive notifications, but they do not have routine access to the corresponding images. The company says this approach addresses concerns about the use of surveillance technology in maritime workplaces. Unlike conventional workplaces, ships also serve as living environments for seafarers. As a result, the use of monitoring equipment raises questions about privacy alongside operational safety. EVI believes safety technology should support crews without creating unnecessary surveillance. “I’ve been a seafarer. I know what it feels like to work under pressure, far from home, with your decisions carrying real consequences,” said Vladimir Ponomarev, CEO of EVI Safety Technology. “If we put cameras around a crew, we owe them more than a promise that the footage will be used responsibly. We have to build those limits into the system,” Ponomarev added. EVI calls for crew-focused maritime technology The launch forms part of EVI’s wider effort to promote greater control over the use of AI-powered monitoring systems at sea. According to the company, technology providers should establish clear limits on who can access footage of seafarers. These restrictions should be built into the systems themselves rather than depend only on internal policies. Crew-First Mode is designed to maintain safety alerts while restricting routine shore access to visual records. The company argues that this approach can help balance the operational benefits of AI monitoring with the privacy expectations of crews. EVI has not disclosed how many vessels currently use Crew-First Mode or whether the feature has been adopted by specific shipping companies. Nevertheless, the launch introduces an additional privacy-focused option for operators considering AI camera systems for onboard safety monitoring.

articles.title: ESAB Launches Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC Welder
articles.summary: ESAB has introduced the Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC TIG/Stick welder. The Rogue combines AC/DC TIG welding capabilities with controls that make it easier for welders of all skill levels to optimize arc performance and weld quality. Featuring ESAB’s 5-in.
articles.body: ESAB Launches Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC Welder Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © ESAB ESAB has introduced the Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC TIG/Stick welder. The Rogue combines AC/DC TIG welding capabilities with controls that make it easier for welders of all skill levels to optimize arc performance and weld quality. Featuring ESAB’s 5-in. color TFT graphical interface, the Rogue gives operators precise control over heat input, penetration, puddle characteristics and bead appearance without the complexity typically associated with advanced TIG welding systems. Features include pulsed AC and DC TIG outputs, four AC waveshapes, adjustable AC frequency and amplitude offset, and a TIG sequencer. Options include the new CoolMini 3 water-cooler and Heliarc SR-20 water-cooled TIG torch. With Lift TIG and HF arc starting options, Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC enables users to weld steel, stainless steel, aluminum and other metals in a wide range of applications, including general fabrication, process industries, tube and pipe fabrication, repair and maintenance, and aerospace. For optimized arc starts, users enter the tungsten type and diameter, and the machine will automatically set parameters. The Rogue ET 230iP weighs 42 lbs. (without water cooler) and connects to 115/230V AC primary power for location flexibility. It has a TIG welding amperage adjustable from 5 to 230A DC and 15 to 230A AC. On 230V primary, it has a rated TIG output of 230A at 30% duty cycle and a rated Stick output of 180A at 30% duty cycle for welding with electrodes up to 5/32-inch diameter. The Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC works well for welding aluminum because it provides four AC waveshape options: Square for maximum arc stability and energy transfer. Soft square for a softer arc and more fluid puddle. Sinusoidal for a quieter and traditional arc. Triangle for reduced heat input on thinner material. To further tailor the wave form to the application, the machine also offers adjustable amperage offset. The Rogue ET 230iP also provides an AC frequency control adjustable from 50 to 150 Hz. Higher frequencies produce a narrower, more intense arc cone that helps direct the arc at the root of the joint in a fillet weld. Higher frequencies also narrow bead width and increase penetration and travel speeds. The Rogue ET 230iP provides pulsed TIG AC and DC outputs that are adjustable from 0.5 to 200 Hz (pulses per second). With pulsed TIG, the welding power source pulses the welding current between a high peak current and a low background current, with the background current set as a percentage of peak current. Stainless steel fabricators and those working with thin metals or other heat-sensitive applications can use pulsed TIG to control heat input, narrow the weld bead profile and increase travel speed. The machine also offers a new 4T2 mode that switches the value of the main current to a lower welding current with a quick tap of the torch trigger, then returns it with a second tap. This function helps when welding around corners or edges without stopping the weld.

articles.title: DP World joins Canadian partners to explore new Arctic trade corridor
articles.summary: DP World, Arctic Gateway Group and CentrePort Canada have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore new trade opportunities across Canada’s northern transportation network. Announced on October 26, 2026, the agreement focuses on port operations, logistics services and the potential development of an...
articles.body: DP World, Arctic Gateway Group and CentrePort Canada have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore new trade opportunities across Canada’s northern transportation network. Announced on October 26, 2026, the agreement focuses on port operations, logistics services and the potential development of an integrated trade corridor. The proposed connection would link the Port of Churchill, Hudson Bay Railway, CentrePort Canada and DP World’s global logistics network. The partnership aims to improve access to international markets and strengthen connections between Canada’s inland and coastal transportation infrastructure. It also explores opportunities to connect Europe and Asia through intermodal transportation routes across Canada. Port of Churchill at the centre of proposed trade corridor The Port of Churchill, located on Hudson Bay in northern Manitoba, plays a central role in the proposed partnership. Arctic Gateway Group owns and operates the port and the Hudson Bay Railway. Together, these assets provide a transportation connection between northern Manitoba and the wider Canadian rail network. According to Arctic Gateway Group, the port is handling its most diverse range of commodities to date. These include grain, potash, critical minerals and supplies destined for Nunavut. Meanwhile, discussions are underway to attract private investment for further port modernisation and export growth. The agreement also involves CentrePort Canada, a major inland port and Foreign Trade Zone in Manitoba. Its infrastructure connects businesses through road, rail and air cargo transportation. CentrePort has attracted approximately $1.5 billion in private investment in recent years. More than 1,000 companies operate within the development area. In addition, over 3.5 million square feet of industrial space has been completed or remains under construction over the past eight years. The new partnership will examine how these inland facilities could connect more effectively with Churchill and international shipping networks. DP World to explore logistics connections DP World’s participation brings international port operations and logistics expertise to the initiative. The company handles more than one million TEUs annually in Canada and operates a global network of port terminals and supply chain services. Through the agreement, the three organisations will explore opportunities to improve connections between Canadian exporters and overseas markets. “This agreement is an opportunity to explore how the Port of Churchill, the Hudson Bay Railway and CentrePort Canada can connect more effectively with DP World’s global network and end-to-end logistics capabilities,” said Doug Smith, CEO of DP World in Canada. Smith added that combining the organisations’ infrastructure and expertise could strengthen supply chains and create additional options for Canadian exporters. Chris Avery, President and CEO of Arctic Gateway Group, also highlighted the potential benefits of closer cooperation. According to Avery, better integration between Churchill and Manitoba’s inland transportation infrastructure could support a unified trade corridor. This would help connect Western Canadian resources with new international markets. Carly Edmundson, President and CEO of CentrePort Canada, noted that the partnership could improve access to several existing trade routes. These include the Arctic gateway through Churchill, alongside the Mid-Continent, Asia Pacific and eastern gateways. The agreement comes as Canada seeks to strengthen and diversify its international trade connections. However, the MoU represents an agreement to explore opportunities rather than a confirmed infrastructure investment. The organisations have not announced specific project costs, construction commitments or a timeline for developing the proposed corridor.

October 27, 2026 © Adobe Stock/GoAerials Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile. The Houthis also said they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route. Intensifying hostilities between Yemen and Saudi Arabia have further disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began. The Houthis' military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on the Ras Tanura refinery had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and is located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure. Nearly all Saudi Arabia's oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past. Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal. AIRSTRIKES The Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks. On Tuesday afternoon, civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh. The Houthis said they had repelled an advance by forces they described as Saudi-backed from the southern approaches to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces earlier this month pushed the Houthis out of coastal areas they had seized in September, loosening the group's grip on a vital Red Sea oil route. Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni city of Mocha. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation. The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa. On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to reduce regional tensions. Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the three countries in a mutual defence pact, authorised Egypt's military on Monday to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked. (Reuters)

Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei a day after holding talks with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. Scope for peace has been dented, however, by renewed attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on key oil producer Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said on Tuesday that they had struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. Swiss bank UBS said it expects Brent prices to stay elevated near $110 a barrel through to the end of the year, citing volatile Middle East supply and geopolitical uncertainty. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen but the number of vessel attacks has increased, with risks likely to become more acute if US naval support wavers, UBS said. Brent touched $117 on Monday as well. "The impression now is that there is a significant risk premium in crude oil prices for the risk that the US/Israel will attack Iran in the coming weeks," said SEB analyst Bjarne Schieldrop.
